speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I understand
Mackenzie and Mann are proprietors of Mackenzie and Mann, Limited, but I suo-mit that has no bearing on the question before the House. We are not purchasing the shares of Mackenzie and Mann, Limited. We are about to purchase the shares of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. My own view is that it is not relevant to this discussion to know the names of the shareholders, but on account of the discussion which developed in the House I thought it advisable to place upon the Table the list of shareholders as of record. This transaction, although it is a large one, is a comparatively simple transaction. The Dominion Government is already-and this fact, I am afraid, is lost sight of in this House-the owner of $40,000,000 stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company: that is to say, we are a minority stockholder in that company. There are $60,000,000 par value of shares still outstanding. Instead of continuing assistance to the company, as we have in the past, we say that we will acquire the $60,000,000 of shares outstanding, thus making the Dominion Government the sole shareholder, instead of a minority shareholder of the Canadian Northern. I submit that the question as to who are the shareholders of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited is not relevant to the section now under discussion by the committee, but I express the view, with some confidence that Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann-that is Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann-are the proprietors of Mackenzie and Mann, Limited. But we are not buying their stock.

Therefore, I would think that when, by this Bill, the pledgees are given authority to name one of the arbitrators jointly with Mackenzie and Mann Company, Limited, it would not be unreasonable that the House should be informed as to who those pledgees are, and as to whether or not they received the stock from Mackenzie and Mann Company, Limited.

The Solicitor General informed the House the other night that, as tlo $51,000,000 of the stock held by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, that stock is, with other assets of Mackenzie and Mann, Limited, pledged to the Canadian Bank of Commerce by the company. If my hon. friend were carrying on a large business, having contracts, bonds and stocks of companies, amongst others the stock of a railway company, whether the Canadian Northern or Canadian Pacific, and doing business with his bank, he would know that he would give a pledge in respect of all the assets of his firm. It is not the case, as I pointed out to the hon. member for Edmonton, of a specific lo-an against a specific security. The general balance of account between Mackenzie, Mann and Company and their bankers is, I understand, secured as a general balance of account of any firm is secured, by a pledge to their bankers, including among others, these securities. It has never appeared to me that this question is relevant to the consideration of the section now before the House, because it is for the arbitrators to determine what is a fair value for the shares. If we were buying shares of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and my hon. friend from

St. John was so fortunate as to own $100,000 worth of stock which he pledged with other assets to the bank, it would not occur to me that this House would be desirous of knowing what amount he owed the bank, in [DOT]respect of that pledge. The real question is, shall the Government buy the stock, and secondly, what is the price that should be paid for it? We propose to have the matter determined by arbitration, and our arbitrator is to be the Chief Justice of Ontario.

speechtext:
I do not propose t>o
discuss the question as to the importance of it. It seems to me it could be well argued that Parliament should be informed on that subject. My hon. friend (Sir Thomas White) says that we seem to forget that the Government already owns 40 per cent of the common stock of the Canadian Northern. Let me say that neither this House nor the country is likely to forget that, because, simultaneously with the getting of that stock, the country became committed to the enormous liability of $45,000,000. That is a fact that the country is not apt to forget. Neither is the country apt to forget that because the very next year or the second year after that obligation was entered into, the country is called upon to pay $15,000,000 more into the enterprise-and one of the arguments advanced in favour of it is that the country had previously, in 1914, become committed so enormously by guaranteeing the bonds to the extent of $45,000,000, it could not, without affecting the credit of the country, refuse the additional $15,000,000. Therefore, the country is riot likely to forget the circumstances under which that common stock was acquired, which common stock, I do not hesitate to say, is intrinsically just worth the value of waste paper.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: And my hon. friend recollects that he was in favour of arbitration to determine the value of these shares, fixing for them a maximum of a very large amount?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Yes, I remember, too, that at that time my hon. friend, the Minis-

ter of Finance, assured Parliament that if $45,000,000 were guaranteed the company would be able-he believed he could inform the House with full confidence-to go on and complete its entire system. He said they had $45,000,000 available for all the purposes of the road, and .there was no likelihood of their coming back for further assistance, and the resolution which I had the honour ol moving was to the effect- and my hon. friend forgets that, apparently -that the stock issue should be reduced from $77,000,000 .to $30,000,000, so that, instead of standing at $100,000,000, as the Government proposed it should stand, it should be reduced to $30,000,000, that all of that stock should be placed in the hands of a trustee, for the benefit and security of the people of Canada, and that it should remain there for five years, so that, in case of default, the Government would have power to act upon it, and speedily take possession of the road, without paying out any money; that, in case it was carried on successfully for five years, paid its interest, and its expenses of operation, and became a successful enterprise, this Parliament would have the right-if it was thought desirable to take over the road and have it operated as a Government work- to take the stock by arbitration.
Does not my hon. friend think that the circumstances under which that suggestion was made are very different from the circumstances with which we are confronted to-day? Does my hon. friend forget that in 1914 he assured Parliament that through the remarkable ability and the wonderful and unprecedented ingenuity of the Solicitor General a plan had been prepared which was embodied in section 24 of the Bill, under which Parliament would have the right to foreclose by Order in Council the equity of redemption in the Canadian Northern Railway Company and in all the subsidiary companies, and if Parliament thought fit to do so it would in that way, acquire an absolute title to that property without foreclosure proceedings and without the payment of any more money, but solely in consideration of the enormous sums which had been poured into this railway system in the past, and in consideration of the vital assistance which is being asked for in 1914? Has my hon. friend forgotten all that? Has he forgotten that he said he wanted to take off his hat to the Solicitor General in recognition of the wonderful ability and the great ingenuity which he had displayed in fram-

ing this resolution under -which Parliament could so speedily act in the interests of the people of this country? He must have forgotten all this, because to-day he is telling Parliament and telling the country that it would be nothing short of an outrage to act under the authority which was then given to the Government at the suggestion of those who are now occupying the treasury benches. He says now it would be an outrage to act upon that wonderful provision which was framed by the Solicitor General, and which was proposed by my hon. friend when he asked Parliament to assent to the Bill. I have been drawn away from the question I proposed asking the minister by reason of his referring to circumstances which I think he would be glad to forget in view of the action which he is now asking Parliament to take. My hon. friend says in the statement that there are in the treasury of the province of Saskatchewan something over $1,000,000, and that that is held in trust and will be available for the purpose of completing certain branch lines in that province. I would ask if that is the ease. With reference to all the other current assets mentioned in the statement which has been laid upon the table of the House, each held on account of Dominion Government, $4,471,611.12; province of Manitoba, $239,350.64; province of Alberta, $3,104,966.24; province of Ontario, $407,487.43; province of British Columbia, $6,403,989.06; would all those amounts be amounts that are not payable to the company to-day but would be payable in the event of their completing certain railways in those various provinces? From what the minister says I would assume that to be the case.

When my hon.
friend asked me the question I informed him correctly, although I was not positive of it myself, that the lands in the province of Ontario and the province of Quebeo were not pledged .under the bond mortgages. The lands which were pledged were those in the West to which my hon. friend

has referred. We have no means of knowing the value of those lands. In any event, it would be a matter of estimate. The only means we have of knowing their value would be the sales which have taken place. I laid upon the table of the House and placed upon Hansard a statement showing the sales made, and having regard to the prices obtained from those sales, it would appear that about $15 an acre was the price. I believe that is the price at which their auditors have taken the lands in. I do not say those lands are worth that money. It seems to me that would have to be taken into consideration by the arbitrators appointed, if they regard it as desirable to value the assets of the company. I am not quite able to follow the argument of my hon. friend with respect to those lands, because he seems to suggest that we should leave them out; that we should not take them in at all. That could be done 'only if we repudiated the liability of the bonds which had been issued, secured by them. I understood my hon. friend the other day to suggest that we should do that, that is, that we might not pay the bonds outstanding which had been issued against those land grants by the company, but I would point out to my hon. friend that that part of the debenture debt, although secured by those lands, is the same as any other part of the debenture debt, because the proceeds went into the construction of the railway.

I desire to repeat that this is not the time to pour out these.millions of money to Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann. The Minister of Finance has found the people of Canada so responsive to his demand for taxes that he thinks the people are able and willing to pour their millions freely into the treasury of this country. He forgets that he has made the people of Canada believe that he wanted these enormous sums raised by way of taxation in order to enable Canada to do her part in carrying on this war. The people have never dreamed that these moneys which he has been taking out of their pockets were to be poured into the lap of Mackenzie and Mann-these favourite sons of fortune whose headquarters are in the beloved home of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, the city of Toronto. When the people of this country find that the moneys which they have so freely contributed for the purpose of assisting the country in doing her part in this war are to be given away to these gentlemen, they will entertain a very different opinion. The people of Canada do not understand the iniquitous provisions of this measure at the present time, but the people in the great cities are learning from the newspapers what it means, and before long, if the discussion continues for any length of time, the people throughout the country will know what it means, and a storm of indignation will go up from the Atlantic to the Pacific which I think will astonish even the Minister of Finance.

speechtext:
I shall not attempt to make reply to the purely show features of what I may describe as the speech to the press gallery of the hon. member for St. John. There are, however, serious members of the committee who are anxious that no substantial feature of the subject before us shall be in any way obscure. I have heard the warning of the hon. member for St. John, that we are going to have to	pay	at least	sixty	milliondollars for	this	stock, on	the	determination of	its	value by	the	arbitrators, and he assures the country that the stock is not worth a dollar. He knows that in the height of his wisdom. He has no 
confidence that men like Sir William Meredith, and an appointee agreeable to him or to the Chief Justice of the Exchequer Court of Canada, will be anything but mere victims of the chicanery of Mackenzie and Mann. I do not know that the committee has any reason' to assume that the Chief Justice of Ontario and the Chief Justice of the Exchequer Court would not be proof, and could not select men who would be proof, against the chicanery of Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, -just as much >as the hon. member for St. John is proof against it. I have no reason to assume that such men would be mere putty and clay in the hands of the Canadian Northern any more than the hon. member for St. John would be putty >and clay in the hands of either the Canadian Northern or the Canadian Pacific.
As to these land grant bonds, I do not know what the hon. member for St. John has in the back of his head. I do not know what he is trying to express. I have not been able to get my mind around any complete idea that he is trying to give the committee. What are these land grant bonds? The Canadian Northern Railway Company became the possessors of a large grant of land. It formerly belonged to Mackenzie and Mann, then to Mackenzie-Mann, Limited and, in return for stock, it became the property of the company. The Canadian Northern then were the owners of more than 4,000,000 acres of land in Western Canada. What happened? The Canadian Northern Railway Company issued land grant bonds and secured them on that land grant.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: In the West?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Yes, they are all in Western Canada. There was, first, a land grant bond issue of $7,000,000, the proceeds of which were applied to the Canadian Northern Railway, just the same as the proceeds of every other bond issue of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. Then, subsequently, they issued another, but not being able to secure as much money as they desired to get for the purposes of the railway on that land grant, what did they do? They procured Mackenzie and Mann to put in the townsites as additional securities and the townsites were then added'to the security of the land grants and the whole was made the basis for another issue the proceeds of which also went into the road. The committee must remember that these bonds were the bonds of the Canadian Northern Railway Com-

pany, were the promissory notes of the company which they are obliged to pay and which can be got rid of by one method and one method only and that is lepudia-tion. No other method in the world can get rid of them. No mere construction of words will get rid of them. You may repudiate them, of course, but that is the only way. Other issues of bonds have beau made since then. Vi hat are those sub ie-quent issues? They are issued guaranteed by the Government, there are mortgages made on the road, tnd which are made to secure the money that we have advanced. There is the consolidated bond issue. What is the po3.tion of the securities? My hon. friend assumes that the land grant is not worth nearly as much as what is against it. I do not think he is at all correct. Even if we could in honour or law repudiate this debt, where would we be? We would, of course, lose the security. What is the fact? My hon. friend says that these lands are just the tail end, the leavings of the original lands. I am afraid he does not understand the way lands are sold by railway companies in the West. It is not as if a farmer comes along, looks at a piece of land and says: " I will take that " and another farmer comes along and says: " I will take that" with the result that after the good land has been picked out you have only the worst land left. That is not the procedure at all. They put values on that land in accordance with the quality and location of the land, the values which they think the land ought to have. There is just as likely to be good land left as good land sold. Then, it comes down to a question of the fairness of the value put upon the land by the company. Instead of the sales of land indicating that it is valueless, they indicate the very opposite. Valuations arrived at by lands actually being sold now show a tremendous equity in these lands, amounting to several millions of dollars. Lands have been sold at the following rates:

I would point out that the increased rate at which they have been able to sell these lands indicate that the proportion of good land left is about the same as it was at the beginning. I only make that argument as a matter of inference, I do not make it as a matter of personal knowledge but clearly from the record it would appear that the land that is left is likely to be a fair average of the land that has been sold. At all events the land generally is much higher in value now than it was. That is a fair assumption, based on recent sales, and consequently if we adopt a scheme which would dishonour the obligations of the Canadian Northern the proceeds of which obligations went into this railway, we would in all likelihood forfeit assets of tremendous value. As to taking the valuation of the land; no doubt that would be part of the duty of the arbitrators. We are getting the land as a part of the property of the railway company and consequently it would be for the arbitrators to ascertain

what the land is worth. The Drayton-Acworth commission did not pretend to do that. They did not deem it their duty and I think rightly so but the arbitrators now, no doubt, would find out what these lands are worth. My hon. friend harks back again on the question: Why did you not value the land? We have done it in substance and in effect. We have not valued it specifically. Why? Because to value it specifically would mean for the time being at all events the disintegration of the system. The entity of the company would be destroyed. While the company might exist, it would not own the railway. It was an accepted principle that if we should fix any terms or conditions for ascertaining the value, it would subject us to the application of every rule of law which would tell against the Government and against the people of Canada, as against the plan, the parallel line, which we are following, and which puts us in a much stronger position before the arbitrators especially when we are taking the stock instead of the assets themselves.

Then why did the hon. gentleman vote to arbitrate on it in 1914? We have perhaps the strongest tribunal which the personnel of this country can provide to determine the value of this stock. I know that the people of Ontario have confidence in the Chief Justice of Ontario, and that no agitation which hon. gentlemen may try to engender in this country will ever shake the confidence of that province in the Chief Justice. I believe the people of every other province of Canada have equal confidence that that Chief Justice will not submit the name of a third arbitrator or submit to the name of a third arbitrator who is not strong, true, capable and fair, and if they do not agree on a third arbitrator, then the Chief Justice of the Exchequer Court names the third arbitrator, so the people of this country are secure that there will be strong, capable, able men, who will be able to protect the interests of Canada when this goes to arbitration. What more do the people of Canada ask? We are told that the cities of Canada-the word was very indefinite

are becoming opposed1 to this legislation. I have heard of some talk in one city, but not in any other.

speechtext: I think I had better read the article just as it is. It is in the Montreal Gazette which, by the way, of late particularly, has girded up its loins in Toryism, and is writing very strong articles on almost everything, against Liberalism and in favour of its friends.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Let me read this article, just to be sure that this is hot really just a local objection, and ascertain by reading the article the contents and value of the deliverance of these men. I submit that the deliverance is by very important men, and if it be an important deliverance, we have a combination that ought to carry great weight. The article reads:
The following criticism of the policy of the Government in respect of the Canadian Northern Railway is made:
The Government Bill to authorize the purchase by it of the capital stock of the Canadian Northern Railway is half way through the House of Commons and will shortly be in the Senate. If it becomes law, it will impose on Canada, at a time when the country is under an unprecedented strain, a burden of

unknown magnitude. One certainly greater than any ever before imposed upon this country, with the exception of the war debt.
The purchase of a defined piece of railway property is one thing. The buying of stock in a company with unascertained assets and unknown liabilities is another. Once the Government becomes the principal owner of the common stock, it must provide out of loans or taxes for all the debts of the railway due or to become due and for all future losses in operating. The estimates of expenditure still necessary to be made run into enormous figures. No one knows what the real extent of its obligations are. The railway has bonds outstanding and debts unpaid; so have its subsidiaries. There are guarantees given by it to other companies, unpaid balances on contracts and upon accounts, but to what extent is unknown. What its assets are is equally unknown. It operates and is interested in railway companies, land companies, telegraph companies, tunnel companies, lumber com

panies and hotel companies, but no one knows how far it owns them, what their assets or liabilities are, nor to what extent the railway company is responsible for their liabilities.
No other railway company nor any other group of business men would consider such an acquisition except after elaborate examination and reports from accountants and appraisers on the assets and liabilities, and then only subject to a solvent guarantee that all supposed assets would be delivered and that no undisclosed debts or obligations would appear. To find out these things, where such examination and guarantee cannot be had, the usual course in the United States has been to place the road in the hands of a receiver, whose staff can ascertain them and place them before those interested an accurate and' clear statement. Systems quite as large, notably the Union Pacific, the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe and the Rock Island, have in the United States been through this process and have emerged from it with capital written down to correspond to the actual values, in a solvent condition and able to perform their duties as public servants.
The only examination so far had into the affairs of the Canadian Northern has resulted in the opinion of two out of three railway experts that the stock proposed to be purchased was worth nothing. This means that whatever its nominal value may be, the unsecured debts are more than enough to prevent its being sold to any reasonably prudent purchaser. In view of the fact that no money was paid to the company-
That should read "paid by" the company, I think.
-for the stock and that the company has never been able to earn anything upon it, there was and is no reason to expect any other result from examination.
No agreement or obligation to purchase Is (produced. In fact, nothing has transpired except verbally and then between members of the Government not named and persons whose names are not disclosed. In fact what is to be paid, who is to get paid for it, what the cost and the attendant obligations are, no one knows. The smallest transaction in common life could not be concluded in such a way, and any attempt to do it by trustees responsible to a court would unquestionably be a

breach of trust, and this is the largest and most onerous undertaking ever contemplated by any Canadian Government, and the most risky. It is safe to say that no road capitalized above its earning power can ever be a useful public servant, nor can any road bought by a government for more than its worth ever be anything but a continuous drain on the taxpayer.
The Canadian Northern Railway was built as a private speculation. Its bonds were sold to financiers at a disoount No money was received into its treasury for its stock. Nothing has been made public which would justify the taxing of other citizens of this country for the purpose of giving fictitious value to these* bonds and stocks. The interest and other charges on Canada due to the war increase every day and even now are so great that it is difficult to say from what source they can be paid without an economic strain never hitherto undergone and a cutting down of expenses not yet even begun.
The credit of the country abroad is less than it has ever been. The last loan of $100,000,000 at 6 .per cent for two years netted only $96,111,111. In other words, the country is borrowing money at a charge of more than 8 per cent per annum. Note.-According to the Hamilton Times of August 17, Sir Thomas White stated the net proceeds to be $96,250.000, not $96,111,111, and that the commissions and charges were 13 per cent. He was speaking of a two-year 5 per cent loan. The cost would be 8 per cent if the 13 per cent comes out of the $96,250,000, but not otherwise. Its future credit may depend entirely on the belief of foreign bankers that good money will not be sent after bad, and that speculative enterprises will be allowed to find the financial level called for by their intrinsic merits.
The undersigned, all of whom as investors, have a stake in the prosperity of this country desire to call the attention of their fellow-countrymen to the grave risk they all are running of having their own earnings diverted for the purpose of securing profits to bondholders and stockholders of a concern, the equity in whose enterprise has been declared by the only people at all in a position to form an opinion to be of no value. It is also urged that the strongest possible protests be made before it is too late to all senators and members of Parliament.
Montreal, August 20, 1917.

Meredith, C. S. Campbell, W. R. Miller, George Caverhilt, Wm. McMaster, H. W. Blackwell, Andrew J. Dawes, Robert Hampson, George R. Hooper, George W. Sadler, W. W. Hutchison, Wm. C. Finley, F. H. Wilson, G. F. Benson, A. Craddock Simpson, James Morgan.
This is a statement made by very prominent businese men of Montreal, and I imagine the majority of them, from what I know, usually look with pleasure on the actions and conduct of this Government.
I would not say that they do so at present. I think, perhaps, they are wavering a little now that some matters have been exposed,

but, generally speaking, I think the majority of these men are supporters of the Government. They are evidently strongly opposed to the taking over of the Canadian Northern, and particularly to the manner of taking it over. On page 8 of the Gazette appears an editorial headed "The Railway Policy," which I will read to the House.

speechtext:
This editorial refers to the meat of the whole thing. It is fair to say that the Montreal Gazette is opposed to government ownership of public utilities.
I will read the editorial:
The Railway Policy.
We print in another column a protest against the purchase of the Canadian Northern Railway signed by many of the leading capitalists of Montreal, and this protest-is not lightly to be disregarded. The point at issue Is this, is the country to take over a burden that other shoulders should bear? Will the ownership of the Canadian Northern impose upon the people a financial obligation avoidable without danger to national interests? If the Government was divorced from the enterprise, the answer is easy. Like any other business undertaking the property should stew in its own juice, and' undergo the course of liquidation through receivership, emerging therefrom in stronger condition in respect of liabilities both of current and of capital account. That appears to be the view of the financiers whose statement we print, and there is, force in the view.
The Canadian Northern must be carried on as an operating road. It serves a great territory and a large community of people whose welfare is dependent upon the operation of this railway, but having exhausted its financial resources the alternative of Government ownership by acquisition of the common stock, or through the medium of a receivership is the only one presented.
To Government ownership we are opposed. A reorganization of the capital liabilities, through the medium of receivership is the other resource. The liability of Canada in either event remains, the Government and the provinces having guaranteed the great sum of $211,000,000 of bonds of the company. It is, however, necessary to learn the extent of the liability taken over by Canada in the Bill now before Parliament. What assets are acquired? What obligations incurred? If there be a margin on the debit side of the account, if Canada is assuming a debt over and above existing guarantees, the public may not unreasonably ask why. The railway is a fine property with excellent prospects, but after all is said, it is a business venture, which should be allowed to face the consequences of all business ventures. One thing is certain; the country should not be saddled with any avoidable liability. The debt created by the war is already large, and constantly increasing. New sources of taxation have to be tapped. TIhe outlook is by no means bright in respect of the Dominion finances and before the additional obligation of taking over the Canadian Northern Railway is incurred, it is necessary at the least that we should know precisely what is being purchased in the way of asset, and what is being incurred in the way of liability.
Having read those two articles to place the viewpoint referred to toy the Solicitor General and the hon. member for St. John before the committee, I can only say the case might have been fairly met had the Government proceeded under the statute of

1914, as I submit they have not, without introducing this new legislation to provide for the payment of equity which is declared to have no value, and which I cannot but believe the statute of 1914 contemplated would not be of value. If that Act were relied upon to obtain possession of the Canadian Northern we would have been pursuing the course outlined in 1914, a course which I believe every member of Parliament thought would have been pursued in the event of default.

speechtext: My hon. friend has read two articles from the Montreal Gazette, with reference to this Canadian Northern purchase Bill. The Gazette article states that the Government has no knowledge of the assets and liabilities of this system. That statement is absolutely incorrect in every particular. The Comptroller of the Railway Department has been through the books of the Canadian Northern Railway system time and again. In 1914 we had special audits made of the assets and liabilities of the company. If hon. gentlemen will take the trouble to look up the statute of 1914 they will find set out there the stock-holdings and the bond-holdings of the Canadian Northern Railway system which were pledged, with all the undertakings and all the assets of every kind whatsoever of the Canadian Northern Railway system,, with trustees to secure the $45,000,000 bond issue guaranteed by the Dominion Government. Within the last two months we have had one of the best fiftns of auditors in the world, Messrs. Marwick, Mitchell, Peat & Co., make a most careful audit of the entire situation of the Canadian Northern Railway, both as to their assets and liabilities.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Supposing the
Government of Canada was taking over the Canadian Pacific Railway to-morrow, as has been talked of-it has not been put forward by the Government, but it has been talked of through the country-does my hon. friend suggest we should expropriate the physical undertaking of the Canadian Pacific Railway, or should we buy its shares? The only suggestion which has ever been put forward, so far as I know, is that we should buy those shares at a price, or guarantee a certain dividend upon those shares. Supposing we came to ascertain how much we should guarantee as dividend on the shares, or how much we should pay. for the shares, could there be any fairer way devised than to submit the matter to the arbitrament of a board constituted as this board is to be constituted?- There must be some way of reaching a conclusion as to a fair price for whatever the Government is purchasing. That is exactly the position so far as the railway situation in Canada is concerned, and there is no use blinking it. Business men outside cannot understand this situation as the Government understands it, because we have been confronted with it for the last six 'years. It is not a theory; it is a condition. Ever since we have come into power, the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company have been in such a condition that they must have help or they would not be able to go on. There is no question about that. Who is responsible for that?
When it comes down to dealing with what this Government is doing now, let us ask ourselves why we are doing this, and why we are obliged to do it. What is the position of the Government with regard to the railways of the country? The policy of the National Transcontinental, which involved

an expenditure of $200,000,000, and the policy with regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific, in respect of which we have had to bring down grants for millions every year, and in respect of which there is in the Estimates a grant to-day of $7,500,000 to meet one year's shortage; the situation under which we have had to help the Canadian Northern to complete its construction and to carry on-all that has been the result of the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite. I do not wish to be understood as criticising them at this time with regard to these matters. I simply desire to say this, that this Government has been confronted with a situation which it has not brought about, which has been brought about by a policy of a Government which was in power before we took the reins of office, and we have had to deal with that situation as best we can. What are the alternatives with regard to the Canadian Northern Railway system? There are just three. The one mentioned in that article in the Gazette, and mentioned by one or two hon. members in this House, is to appoint a receiver. Both Government and Opposition in this House have time and again stated that they are opposed to that course. Hon. gentlemen opposite, through their leader, have expressly stated, time and again, that a receivership is not to be thought of. The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has taken that position. So far as I know, those hon. gentlemen opposite who have been connected with the late Government, and their followers, have taken that view, namely, that there is not to be a receivership. I think that is a sound view. Sir Henry Drayton and Mr. Acworth thought that was a sound view; they said it would not do to have a receivership of this road. It is idle, at this stage when this Bill is before the committee, to say that we should have a receivership, because both sides of the House, as well as the commission we have appointed, have expressly and distinctly stated that there must be no receivership. Why is that a sound view? It is put forward that in the United States there have been receiverships of railways, but there have been no railways in the United States whose credit have been involved with the credit of the Federal and State Governments in the way in which the credit of this railway is involved. The point is that the credit of the Dominion through its guarantees, and the credit of the provinces, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia, through their guarantees, are absolutely involved with the finances of this railway company, and consequently if we throw the system into liquidation, the most calamitous results would ensue so far as concerns the credit of the Dominion and of the provinces. There is no question about that, and that has been the ground upon which both sides in this House-and after all it is the parties in this House that have to determine policy-have determined against a receivership and against liquidation. Hon. gentlemen say to me: Why do you not foreclose? So far as the equity of the situation is concerned, if an ordinary mortgage is foreclosed, the court usually orders a sale in order to determine if there is any value in the equity of redemption. At common law in the old days, they would foreclose. Equity steps in and says: That is not fair; you must offer the property for sale to see if there is an equity of redemption. In other words, it is equitable that an investigation or sale proceedings should be had, in order to determine whether the owner of a property which is mortgaged are entitled to any equity. Even if we put into effect the legislation of 1914-and I believe I can give the committee good reasons why it should not be put into effect-it is stated in that legislation that we may foreclose, subject to such terms and conditions as Parliament may prescribe.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
If any. I say, it would be open to Parliament and it would be equitable for Parliament to hold just such an investigation as we purpose holding in order to find out if there is any equity. It is nonsense to speak about large sums of money by way of award. What is the position of this company? This company is not earning its fixed charges. It is earning $11,000,000 over its operating expenses, and its fixed charges are $15,000,000. It is therefore, idle to speak of an award running into $25,000,000 or $30,000,000. Is it common sense or good sense? What do Messrs. Drayton and Acworth say? Although they found, as they stated, no existing equity, they said that it would be equitable to allow something to the owners, and they suggested an arbitration for the purpose of determining what amount of stock the present proprietors of this road should have in the Dominion Railway Company which they suggested should be incorporated. I pointed out to the House that, in that report of Messrs. Drayton and Acworth, a perfectly admirable report, an excellent report, thought out most carefully

in all details, they had by inadvertence, overlooked certain assets of the company. I have here a letter from the financial comptroller of railways. I made the statement to the House upon information which he had given to me. His letter, which is dated August 15, 1917, reads:
Dear Sir:-
Referring: to our conversation of this morning in which you asked whether in your remarks in the House of Commons yesterday, as reported in Hansard, pages 4644 to 4648, inclusive, you had correctly conveyed the information which I had previously furnished you, that in the findings of the majority report of the Royal Commission appointed to investigate the railway situation in Canada, that the statement, based on Professor Swain's valuation of the physical property of the Canadian Northern Railway system showing there was no equity, was in error.
I may state that it is quite clear that there is an error in that part of the Commissioners' report; the following assets on the asset side
are omitted:
Cash	$25,000,000
Accounts	receivable	 8,890,000
Operating materials and supplies	 916,000
Earnings,	freight	in transit..	558,000
Lands Assets.
Lands unsold, 3,245,987 acres.
Deferred payments and accrued interest, $6,662,000.
On the liability side, there is a shortage of some $25,000,000.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) G. A. Bell.
I stated expressly to the House the other day, and I state again now, that the difference between book assets and book liabilities is not a test as to the value of the common stock. It hy no means follows that the common stock is at all equal in value to the difference between the assets and liabilities of the company. The best test is earning power, as was pointed out by Professor Swain, and in trying to reach a conclusion as to what arbitrators might fairly adjudge, we must bear in mind that this company, although its future prospects are promising, is not to-day earning' its full bond interest. The Government is confronted with a condition and not a theory. If we do not allow this railway system to go into the hands of the receiver, with all the consequences which I have mentioned, there is only one of two destinies for the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and no hon. member here can dissent from this proposition. If the Canadian Northern Railway Company does not go into the hands of a receiver, there are in Canada only two organizations strong enough to hold it: One is the Dominion Government

and the other is the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. You have three alternatives: receivership and liquidation; ownership by the Government of Canada, or ownership by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
Let us look at the matter from another *standpoint. Apart altogether from the Canadian Northern Railway Company, we are confronted with the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Companies. There is no use in our closing our eyes to the fact that every year we have had to aid the Grand Trunk Pacific to the extent of millions of dollars. What is going to be its future? Are we going to continue, year after year, aiding this railway?
Let us see what lies ahead of the Dominion of Canada. How many railways are we going to have on our hands? We have already the Intercolonial, which is ours. We have the National Transcontinental from Moncton to Winnipeg, which line is ours. The Grand Trunk Pacific railway must come in. There is also the Grand Trunk, which has liabilities in connection with that railway. I do not forecast the future with respect to that situation, but I say that the Grand Trunk Pacific in the West and the National Transcontinental need the Canadian Northern railway in the West to supplement them, if we are going to make them a success. Therefore, whether people are in favour of public ownership or not, the matter comes down to this, that if we are going to carry out the railway policy which has been forced upon us by the situation I have described, we need, in addition to the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk. Pacific, the Canadian Northern railway system in the West.
We need it because the Grand Trunk Pacific has no feeders. Who is responsible for all that? What is the Government to do? Should the Government let the company be wrecked and bought up here and there, bit by bit? No. Looking to the future we know we shall have the Grand Trunk Pacific and we may have other roads. We have the National Transcontinental. And what about the Canadian Northern, which fits into the Grand Trunk Pacific system in the West? Hon. gentlemen opposite have moved resolutions in this House-and the statement I shall make is not going to be a sweeping statement with regard to them, because I believe there are mixed opinions among hon. gentlemen opposite about this

matter; indeed, they have so expressed themselves. Some of them, I believe, are in favour of public ownership; some are opposed to it, and some are in favour of a continuation of aid from year to year. But they have united upon a resolution, and let me say that every word in the article read from the Montreal Gazette by my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) was opposed to the resolution for which he voted the other day in this House. He voted the other day for a resolution under which we were to take over the entire Canadian Northern system, lock, stock and barrel, by foreclosure, 'and in the worst way, not in the best way, as I shall show my hon. friend in a minute. Everything that my hon. friend read from the Montreal Gazette, if he believed it, was a condemnation of his vote the other day, because he voted for taking over the entire system, lock, stock and barrel. But not only that. In 1914 he voted for acquiring the stock in precisely the same way that we are acquiring it now; but he proposed to do it in a more foolish way than we are 'adopting, because he fixed a maximum price of $30,000,000, which we would never have thought for a moment of fixing. Why was the course he took the other day a foolish course as compared with the course we have adopted? We are now in the fourth year of this war. I listen to honourable gentlemen opposite sometimes, talking about money rates. Therd are no better fellows that I know than hon. gentlemen opposite, and when I say that they sometimes fail to realize that we are in the midst of a war I do not mean in any way to impeach their interest in this war, because it is just as great as my own. What I mean is this: Do they realize that we are in the fourth year of this war, and that financial conditions in this world are as they are to-day? They do not. I realize it, because I am brought into contact with it every day, and have to face it. It is true we have to pay a higher rate of interest for money. Why? Because the world has been for years at war; that is the reason why I realize, as I think no other man in this House realizes, that to our financial position we should give the most attentive consideration from day to day, and week to week, and month to month. Do hon, gentlemen opposite think that we on this side of the House desire to take over a railway system unless it is in the public interest to do. so? But what is the alternative? Although we are at war, this railway situation is here 307
and we have to face it. Hon. gentlemen opposite can sidestep it, but we cannot. We have to face it and we lay down this proposition: That so far as the
5 p.m. Canadian Northern system, is concerned, instead of going on paying out $15,000,000 or $20,000,000 every year to make good the shortage and enable them to carry on, we will take over the system for the people of Canada. Back of a good deal of criticsim of this measure-
I do not say back of all the oriticsm-is antagonism to the principle of public ownership, rather than criticism of method. The Dominion of Canada has had quite an experience in public ownership. It owns a great system of railways to-day. It owns the Intercolonial and the National Transcontinental. Throwing our imagination ahead we can eee what lies before us, and the question is, shall we acquire the Canadian Northern system or not? Personally, I believe that in five years' time the Canadian Northern system, in the hands of the Government and financed by the Government, will be a great system, but if we let it go into liquidation we shall lose it to the people of Canada.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: It depends on how much money you squander in connection with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
We won't squander any money in connection with it. If we do not do that, we should have only a straight line of railway from Moncton to Prince Rupert, with no feeders in the West. The hon. member for Carleton is as levelheaded a man as there is in the House, practically speaking, and he knows as well as any man, that a straight line like that is not going to give the results that we should like to see given by a transcontinental system owned by the Government. What did the Drayton-Acworth report say about that? They point out that the Canadian Northern system is vital to the successful operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific in the West, and they also indicate that the Grand Trunk is complementary to the Canadian Northern in the East.
Hon. gentlemen opposite say: Why don't you foreclose and take the physical properties? Hon. gentlemen who put that forward have not thought the matter out. If we were not at war, if we could readily raise $100,000,000, $200,000,000, or $300,000,000 that we do not require for the purposes of war, it would be feasible, but it is not feasible to-day, and I will tell you why. If we foreclose on the .Canadian Northern railway under the mortgage, what do we get? We



get the roadbed and the physical properties of the Canadian Northern Railway company. We also get the stocks and' bonds of the underlying companies; hon. gentlemen have overlooked that. The stocks and bonds of the underlying companies, which are included in the assets of the system as laid before this House, will still be outstanding. So that the difference would be this : Instead of owning $100,000,000 of stock of the Canadian Northern Railway company, which would enable us to control the Canadian Northern railway and all its constituent and subsidiary companies, we should have the physical property of the Candian Northern railway only, and the stocks and bonds1 which are embraced in the trust mortgage which was taken under the legislation of 1914.

They are there and have to be taken care of. How could we get title in fee simple to the properties of the Canadian Northern Railway system, without clearing up the indebtedness? Suppose that under the statute we reorganize; what does that mean? It means creating a new company, and negotiating with the present bondholders of the exist-
ing companies, because the hew company would be a separate entity.

speechtext:
It would be in ordinary times. In ordinary times a complete arrangement could be made to finance the Canadian Northern. The Government could substitute its securities for other securities which run from 20 to 40 years and the situation could be dealt with in that way. It cannot be dealt with to-day at all. It is not possible having regard to the financial condition. Thus, to-day, the proper course to take is the course which preserves /the Canadian Northern Railway company as a corporate organization in order that it may continue its financing. There is a loan of $11,500,000 coming due in New York. The Canadian Northern has to renew that loan in New York. If the Canadian Northern were wiped out as an entity that loan would have to be met, and you would have a
307J
financial situation of some gravity. As far as the course we are adopting is concerned, it is the best course having regard to finance. It is a course which is greatly preferable to foreclosing if the principle is adopted that the equity of redemption, if there is any value in it, is entitled to be valued. If that principle is adopted, and I submit it would be adopted by Parliament, as it is adopted by the courts, that is the most preferable course and it is the course that hon. gentlemen opposite voted for and is practically the same as that which we favour on this side of the House except that the one that we put forward is better from the standpoint of finance to that which they have put forward.
The statement that we do not know what the assets and liabilities are is not correct. We have made a very full investigation. Over a course of years that investigation has been proceeding. Auditors have gone through the books. The accounts of the company have been verified, and will be verified further, as to the financial condition, before any agreement is entered into. This House has ample information upon which to reach a decision upon a question as large as this. If you were taking over a small concern with assets of a few hundred dollars you would examine into everything to the minutest detail. I suppose that could be done. Of course, the Government would never be taking over anything of that kind. An individual would pursue that course but when you are taking over a great railway system like this, if you get at the liabilities, the bonded indebtedness, the floating indebtedness, the physical properties, the bonds, stocks and other securities it holds, and its earning power, you have substantially all the information necessary upon which to form your judgment because this is such a large transaction that you cannot get down to a matter of the uttermost detail.

The minister says that section 24 of the Act of 1914 contained admirable provisions which could be well acted upon if these were not war times. I have read with very great care the remarks which were made by my hon. friend in 1914 when he was seeking to persuade Parliament to authorize the Government to guarantee these bonds to the extent of $45,000,000. I have read his language with regard to the very great advantage it would be to give to the Government the power, or to reserve to Parliament the power, in the form of a statutory agreement

that is what it was an agreement entered into by the Canadian Northern interests-that in case default should be made the Government would be authorized to act and to declare by Order in Council the equity of redemption in all the premises covered by that mortgage to secure the $45,000,000 foreclosed. What further are the premises which are mortgaged in that mortgage to secure the bonds guaranteed by the Government under the legislaion of 1914? They are all the various stocks in the subsidiary companies and the bonds, if there were any, which were held by the Canadian Northern Railway company. They are the premises which are covered by the mortgage, and under the provisions of section 24, the moment the Governor in Council passed that order for foreclosure, the equity of redemption would be absolutely wiped out and His Majesty would become the owner of the system. speechtext: No, I am not suggesting that. For the moment I am meeting the suggestion of the Finance Minister to the effect that these obligations, being outstanding, would in some way embarrass the Government if it acted under section 24 and became the owner of the system, or was obliged to form a new company. Having become the owner of the system under the authority of section 24, and having formed the new company, what -would the Government do? It would at once inquire into the securities which it had taken over under that order. It would find a certain number of valuable securities in the city of New York -securities guaranteed by the Governments of the Dominion and of the different provinces. It would find certain loans had been made against these securities. I ask you, Sir, if the new company, known to be a company acting for Hie Majesty, would have any more difficulty in securing a renewal of those loans than the Canadian Northern Railway company itself would have? Would not its security be as good as or better than that of the Canadian Northern Railway company? It would own all the property the Canadian Northern Railway company owns today, and the company would be a new one free from all entanglements and obligations of every kind and description, and having at its back the Government of Canada, as representing His Majesty the King. Yet the minister says this new company, organized under those circumstances, would have difficulty in renewing its short-term obligations held by the bankers of New York against absolutely good guaranteed securities. The minister has formed the idea, based upon something I do not understand, that if section 24 were acted upon it would give somebody an opportunity to put some company into the hands of a receiver. subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I thought the minister had in view the land grant bonds. Surely the minister meant-certainly his language would lead one to believe that he meant that, if section 24 were acted upon and the equity of redemption were foreclosed by Order in Council, there would necessarily arise a condition of affairs under which creditors would be able to put the system into the hands of a receiver. I am glad the minister did not mean that. I did not see how such a result would follow. Of course, I realize, and every one realizes, that, if the Government became the owner of the equity of redemption by virtue of an' Order in Council, foreclosing under an agreement entered into in 1914, and if the Government did not pay the interest upon the obligations against that property,
. there would be a receivership, and there would be a foreclosure of those mortgages. My answer to that is this: that the Government could, in the name of His Majesty, become the owner of the property under an Order in Council barring or foreclosing the equity of redemption, and then be, so far as all those outstanding securities are concerned, in exactly the same position as the Canadian Northern is in to-day. If any of those bonds run for 40 years, they would still run for 40 years; if any of them run for 20 years, they would still run for 20 years. Therefore, there would be no inconvenience whatever, but on the contrary, there would be the advantage of having a new company with a new organization, which would be acting for His Majesty under the provisions of the statute of 1914.
What would we get rid of in that way? We would get rid of the probability of having to pay out an enormous sum of money under this arbitration to the holders of the stock of the Canadian Northern. Is that not something to get rid of? Some honourable gentlemen opposite argue that it would be confiscation to take that course. Surely, it would not be confiscation to carry out an agreement that has been entered into. Suppose a man has a mortgage on my property and the interest upon it amounts to the rental and the taxes and the cost of repairs, and I go to him and say: 'I want to borrow $5,000 more upon the property; I have faith and believe that I can carry the thing through;
I agree that if you will lend me $5,000 you can take charge of the property if I make default in the payment of the interest; I will hand you an agreement releasing my [Sir Thomas Whited
equity of redemption in the property; it is yours, without your being obliged to take any proceedings for foreclosure or putting the property up for sale. I act upon the agreement and the mortgagor acts upon it. Could I isay afterwards that I was treated most shamefully because my agreement was simply carried out in the letter and in the spirit in which I made it? Is not that exactly the same position as between Mackenzie, Mann and Company and His Majesty, as represented by the Government of the day? After they have received millions and millions of the public moneys Mackenzie, Mann and Company ask for further assistance. They said to this Government " Give us the assistance and if we do not pay the interest upon the money, if we make default in any respect, we agree that Parliament may authorize you, simply by Order in Council, without any legal proceedings whatever, to bar our equity in the property and take over and become the absolute owners of the system." That was the agreement, and all we ask is that it be carried out.

The committee resumed at eight o'clock, Mr. Kainville in the Chair.
Mr. PUGSLEY Mr. Chairman, just before recess I was speaking of what I thought was the untenable position taken by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance that if this railway system was acquired in any other way than by taking over this stock, it might lead to complications. I thought I largely answered that argument of my hon. friend. Indeed, I understood that he admitted that there would not be any complications arising with respect to a new company, if the Government acted under section 24 of the statutes of 1914 and foreclosed equity of redemption under the statutory agreement, and that if a new company were organized by the Government it would stand in a position just as good as that of the Canadian Northern Railway company. In the one case the Government would own all the stock of the new company and in the other case, by virtue of this Bill, the Government would simply own the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway company. I was endeavouring to deal with the question from the standpoint of the Government taking over the system and becoming liable for the underlying obligations. Of course, if the Government were simply to expropriate the property

and have it valued by the judge of the Exchequer Court, I have very little doubt, from the evidence which we have as to the actual cost of the road, that the Government would get the system for a great deal less money-for many millions less than is represented by the existing securities. There are something like $147,000,000 of securities which are not guaranteed by either the Dominion or any of the provinces. I presume these securities are held by strong financial men, by bankers and others who could afford to lose a portion of their securities just as well as the country could afford to pay them money which is not represented by the system. But, if the Government decide that it is better, for reasons connected with maintaining the public credit, to pay this $147,000,000 of obligations which are unsecured by any public authority, a proposition with which I do not at all agree, when it does seem to me that the road ought to be taken under the authority of the statute of 1914 and under the statutory agreement which was then made, instead of taking a step which means in all human possibility-indeed I think, necessarily means-handing out a great many more millions of the money of the people of Canada to Messr-i. Mackenzie and Mann and their associates.
I am sorry that I did not have an opportunity of hearing the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) this afternoon, as possibly he referred to the remarks which I had made. I was obliged to leave the Chamber to attend a committee meeting. But I shall have an opportunity of seeing his remarks in Hansard, and possibly there may be an occasion later on in the discussion of the Bill when I can give attention to his observations in case they seem to require some reply from me.
The Minister of Finance gives an extraordinary reason for taking over the Canadian Northern Railway system. When he seemed to fail in argument as to the reason for this extraordinary step upon other grounds, he said: "Why, Mr. Chairman, we must look ahead; there is a great transcontinental railway system extending from Moncton to Winnipeg already owned by the Government, and built with Government aid from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean; it is capable of being a great railway system, and the Government must take it over in the near future." That is the effect of what my hon. friend said, but, he added: "That road has no branch lines," or, "that road is lacking in branch lines, and we want the Canadian Northern
railway in order to supplement the Grand Trunk Pacific system." Is it to be suggested for one moment that this Government is to be plunged into an obligation of $500,000,000 and upwards in order to secure a system of branch lines for the Grand Trunk Pacific? Did any one ever hear of such an extraordinary suggestion? It will be better to wait until the Government acquires the Grand Trunk Pacific system, and then build all the branch lines necessary to tap the country north and south. You could build all the branch lines you want in the Canadian West, even at present prices of labour and materials, for $20,000 a mile. For $40,000,000 you could build 2,000 miles of branch lines to feed the system of the Grand Trunk Pacific. But, instead of that, my hon. friend suggests, as [DOT]a reason why we should take over the Canadian Northern Railway system and bind the country to this vast obligation, that we want branches in order to feed the Grand Trunk Pacific system. If that is the best reason my hon. friend can give, I do not think his proposal will give very much satisfaction to the people of this country.
There is another reason why this measure should not be pressed. It is taking a very great departure; it is providing for the government ownership of a great railway system. This question has never been submitted to the people. Speaking for the people of my own province, I am satisfied I represent their opinion when I say that they are not in favour of imposing this vast obligation upon the Canadian public at the present time. I deny the right of this moribund Parliament- this Parliament which died a constitutional death nearly a year ago, and which is in existence to-day, not by the votes of 'the people, but simply by our own votes, and as the result of a resolution which we passed requesting the Imperial Parliament to extend our parliamentary term-to commit the people of Canada on this question. This moribund Parliament has no mandate from the people to impose upon them an obligation of $500,000,000 and upwards, which is but the beginning of the financial obligations which will be imposed by reason of the acquisition of this system. It h<*s no constitutional or moral right to do it.
I must not detain the committee, because I know there are many hon. gentlemen on this side of the House who desire to speak. Hon. gentlemen on the other side who may feel constrained as supporters of the Gov-

eminent to give their adherence to this extraordinary measure will want to explain to the people why they are prepared to take that course. The people will demand from them an explanation on the floor of this House of their reasons for so doing. There are hon. gentlemen on this side who would deem it to be their duty to call the attention of Parliament and of the people to the objectionable proposals which are now under consideration.
I regret very much indeed that a measure so important and so far-reaching in its consequences, involving the people in tremendous obligations at this time when the country requires its full credit in order to raise the moneys which are necessary to carry on the war, should be brought down so late in the session.
It is over seven months since Parliament first met, and this measure might have been presented for consideration long ago. It is impossible to properly consider it before the expiry of the life of this Parliament. It might be well for the minister to have printed for circulation the statements which he presented a few days ago. Time should be given in order that the people of Canada may become acquainted with all that this measure means. They have not had time for that yet and that time cannot be given if this measure is to be put through before the extended life of this Parliament expires. The people are becoming aroused, and as they become more fully acquainted with the measure, I am satisfied that the feeling against it will become stronger and stronger.

I am glad my hon. friend has asked that question because it shows, if I may say so without offence, an entire misconception of the transaction. If we expropriated the Canadian Northern Railway system, took over all the physical properties and paid1 off the indebtedness, then we should have to raise a very large amount to do it, but that is precisely what we are not doing and what it would be very unwise, or I might say impossible, to do at this time. I pointed out on a previous occasion that the Canadian Northern Railway debt is pretty well funded, that is to say the securities have been issued for a long period of years, maturing twenty, thirty or forty years from now. That is the principal part of the debt. One advantage that we get from maintaining the corporate organization of this company is that we do not have to raise money to pay off the indebtedness as shown by these balance sheets. The Dominion Government simply becomes the sole shareholder of the company and the company goes on financing just as in the past.
Another point is that the Dominion Government is not brought into privity with its creditors, legally speaking. It is a mistake to say that the Dominion debt is added to, speaking legally and strictly, because it is not. We are acquiring $60.000,000 of stock in addition to the $40,000 000 we have, so that we shall be the owners of $100,000,000 of fully paid-up stock in the Canadian Northern railway which concern will continue to run as a corporation. Its obligations will be the obligations of the Canadian Northern railway as they are to-day. But the Dominion Government will, of course, help it to run. If the Dominion took over the Canadian Pacific railway to-morrow it would not have to raise money to pay off all the funded indebtedness of the system; it would run it as a corporation, and the earnings of the road would take care of the bonded indebtedness and

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I must say that I cannot consent, as a member of this House, to the people I represent becoming the purchaser of nothing-according to the Government- for which we will have to pay a very large sum of money. This proposed purchase of 600,000 shares of stock which will involve obligations running into hundreds of millions-advancing money constantly to a company, gradually, as the minister says, not all at once-is a policy I could not conscientiously support. I do not intend to speak often in committee on this subject, but I want to place myself on record as saying that this, to my mind, is about the worst transaction the Government has ever
entered into. I say that with all respect to the Government. I mean that it is the worst in the value that the Government is receiving for wrhat it is purchasing. To sum up the whole situation, it seems to me to resolve itself into this. It is apparent that we are getting something, but what that something is the Government do not know and cannot tell us. We are going to pay something for that something; to whom we are going to make payment the Government does not know or will not tell us. We are going to pay a certain amount for that something, how much the Government does not know or will not tell us. We are going to get something apparently of value-or else we would not buy it-what the value is the Government does not know or will not tell us. We are going to assume debts and obligations; to what extent the Government does not know or will not tell us. Apart from the debts we are going to assume, and the values we are going to get-if we get anything of value-we are going to become purchasers of 600,000 shares of stock, but the Government cannot, tell what it is worth. The Government is going to arbitrate, and has named its arbitrators. Other arbitrators will be named, and we will pay the amount that arbitration will fix for that stock. We will assume that liability, in addition to the other liabilities and debts of the company. Where we are going to get the money to pay these liabilities, the Government has not told us. It is well known that money is very expensive; rates of interest are extremely high; we are obliged now to impose taxes upon the people of this country in every shape and form; we require every possible resource of this country towards the winning of the war. We have imposed an income tax for that purpose. The Government is asking the people to assume terrific obligations under this measure; to what extent they cannot say; and this at a time when the people are hardly able to bear the obligations imposed upon them by the war. I say emphatically that I want to see this country developed along sound lines. I want to see every resource of this country utilized to the advantage of the people and to the advantage of Great Britain and the Allies; I want to see a proper and sound programme carried on by the Government of this country; and for one, I am not prepared to give my consent, on behalf of the people I represent, to the assumption of liabilities and debts for something which apparently is valueless, or the value of which the Government cannot tell us.

Before leaving section 1, I should like to call the attention of the minister to the fact that he has not given us the information I asked for when we were in committee before, as to the names of the pledgees of the stock. That is a matter of very great importance, in view of the fact that, under the Act of 1914, Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, the contractors, covenanted with the Government to give up all possible claims which they might have for commission and otherwise. It is important to know who the pledgees of the stock are, and when the stock was pledged with them. For, if it was pledged since the Act of 1914, the pledgees of the stock, as a matter of law, would have no better or greater title than the original owners of-the stock had; and by reason of the fact that the Act of 1914 was a public statute, they would be bound to know the law, and their rights would he subrogated to' the rights of the original holders. They are therefore, in no better position than the original holders. One of the terms of the agreement ratified by the Act of 1914 reads as follows:
The contractors covenant that they will not at any time make or seek to enforce any claim tor contractors' profits, commissions or otherwise against the Canadian Northern or against any of the constituent or subsidiary companies, upon or in respect of any express or implied contract, understanding,, agreement, or stipulation of any kind, heretofore or hereafter made, whereby or whereunder they, or any one or more of them, may now or hereafter be entitled to receive from the Canadian Northern, or from any of the constituent or subsidiary companies, any construction profits in respect of work heretofore undertaken, or as consideration for transfers of properties rights or franchises already transferred, or to be transferred under sub clauses (a) and (b) of this clause, or for commission or remuneration .for services in financing, or for any other services heretofore rendered, and all such claims are hereby by them and each of them absolutely renounced and released.
The Drayton-Acworth Report says:
The property investment of the Canadian Northern Railway system is stated in the balance sheet of June 30, 1916, at $494,112,489.34. This figure admittedly has been written up to include $100,000,000 of capital stock. And this stock, as we have already said, was issued without any cash consideration.
I called the attention of the minister, as a matter of law, to the fact that this $100,000,000 of stock, the value of which is to be arbitrated under .the proposal of my hon. 
friend, has ibeen found by the commission appointed by himself to have been issued without, any cash consideration, and the suggestion in this report that anything should go to the holders of the stock is based upon the theory merely that they had spent a good deal of time in connection with the matter and were entitled to something by way of honorarium. But whatever right they had on that ground wa3 relinquished under the provisions of the agreement of 1914, and the stock not having been issued for value, as evidenced by the statement in the report of the commission- and also by the statement of my hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Nickle) in 1914 that the whole of the stock of the Canadian Northern was simply watered stock-the result is that the pledgees of the stock have no rights whatever as a matter of law, and the owners of the stock have no rights whatever as a matter of law, they having covenanted not to make any claim on the Government in any way for any services or any conditions such as are shown in the clause I read. The minister should tell us who are the pledgees of this stock; in whose hands the stock is at the present time; for what it was pledged, and when it was pledged-because the first section which he asks the committee to allow to stand is the section that provides for paying money to certain pledgees. I submit, this House has no right to enter at this time into an agreement with some party or parties unknown who are stock pledgees, if the Government know-as they must know-the names of the parties so described, and if, as a matter of fact, those parties have no higher or greater rights than the original holders of the stock in 1914. My hon. friend will recall I asked him for that information, and he ought to give it to us.
