The point is this -and the hon. member from Pictou knows it as well as I do, if not better, because he is a practising lawyer-'that this is an ordinary deposit agreement under which stock is to 'be acquired. The pledgee has a limited interest, because the owner has transferred the stock to him in consideration of a certain advance. Now, in order, to get that stock we have to get it under the terms of this agreement. The owners

and pledgees should lodge it, and if they do not lodge it the agreement does not become operative. If they lodge it, whether owners or pledgees, then it (becomes subject to the terms of the agreement, which are .that the value is to be determined by arbitrators, and when so determined is to be paid over to the proper parties. Who are the proper parties? It is so elementary that I hate to trouble the House about it; the hon. member knows there is nothing in it, but he is raising it simply for the purpose of discussion. He knows perfectly well if owners and pledgees bring their stock into the agreement-the stock so bought by the Government at a price to be fixed by arbitration-the pledgees are in a position to transfer that stock into their names and make themselves the legal owners. As a matter of fact, it was not absolutely necessary that the word " pledgees " should be in the Bill at all.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Why mention it then?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: It was not necessary. I am talking to a committee of business men and good lawyers. Everybody here knows that if stock is pledged to an institution it is within the power of that institution to transfer the stock into its name, and obtain legal ownership of it. The man who transferred it to the institution has an equity interest in it, but the legal ownership is in the institution. The word " pledgee " is not necessary, but .it does no harm. Take the case of a government expropriating real property, and assume there is a mortgagee, has not the mortgagee a right to come in and be heard?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
But he is the registered owner, because he has registered his mortgage in the registry office. Speaking in a strict sense, I say that gives him, as my hon. friend knows, legal title, because the property has been conveyed to him under the law, say, of Ontario-I know that is the case in that province. If a pledge of stock is given to an individual or an institution, it is open to that individual or institution to transfer that stock into his or its name on the books of the company. That individual or that institution then becomes the legal owner. The fact that pledges are mentioned in this makee no real difference, but there is no real objection to it because there are two parties unquestionably interested in stock:

First the man who has pledged the stock, because he may pledge it for only a part of its value, although if he pledges it for its full value, he is liable under the covenant and is interested in his security, but there is no objection to the holder and the pledgee being mentioned in the agreement because the pledgee is entitled to put it in his own name. The matter is so elementary that I do not want to discuss it.

The minister has not given and will not give us the information for which we are asking. able time discussions which are becoming, to say the least of it, somewhat prolonged. We are in the eighth month of this session of Parliament, and the matter is becoming serious to some of us who think we could do more for the war by pitching sheaves than by listening to the same thing said so many times over. I rose for the purpose of saying that I listened with the utmost care to what appeared to me to be a very lucid and convincing statement by the Minister of Finance this afternoon on the general question, and I am persuaded in my mind that, when the people of this country read that statement in connection with the statement made the other day by the Solicitor General, they will come to the conclusion that in this legislation the Government is making an honest effort towards a proper solution of a problem of enormous magnitude and seriousness. That is my honest conviction about the object of the Government and about what the people of the country will think about it.
It is usually said that there are three possible solutions of our railway difficulties. I have a fourth which has never, been mentioned in the course of these debates, and I do not suppose that my mentioning it will carry much conviction, but it would be a solution if it could be arrived at. My solution of the railway difficulty is to make the railways pay. It would not matter much whether they belonged to the Government or to private companies if they were paying concerns. You can make them pay only by making them do business, and to do business is to trade. If you will allow our railroads to trade freely, they will do more business; they will make more money, and they will pay. Of course, when I put the matter in that way, I think I should carry a great deal of conviction to both sides of the House; but if I reverse the words and speak about free trade, I should at once be looked upon as a kind of mountebank. I am afraid that is too strong meat for either side of the House just yet, and I am, therefore, bound to take the current opinion that there are only three possible solutions of this question. I feel, as a patriotic Canadian, proud of the country of my adoption in which I expect my grand-children and my grand-children's children to be brought up with future generations, that there is no upstanding Canadian who wants to face the question of a receivership. Some hon. members spoke about a receivership being a bogey. I never suffered from bankruptcy, but I should not think that bankruptcy is any /

bogey. It is a bad thing for an individual, and it will be a very much worse thing for this nation at a time when we are facing problems of magnitude greater than any that have been, dreamed of since Confederation, and when we wish to keep the credit of our country as high in the financial world as our soldiers have put it in the military world upon the field of battle.
With regard to the second possible solution of this question, which has not been without support from my own. side of the House in the course of this debate, namely, the handing out of more money to the Canadian Northern, I am perfectly sure that the people of this country who give any thought to the subject at all are sick of that process. They do. not want to shovel out any more money to private individuals for the running of this road, and the reason is not far to see. It is an interminable process which does not seem to get us any further forward, and in addition to that, it has this cardinal objection, that there is a very sound suspicion in the minds of our people that the money does not all by any means find its way into the railroad. The people are sick of that process.
Then, what is to be done with the situation? We are brought to the third possible solution.-the solution which the Government, as I believe, in good faith, are trying to take-and that is the nation must take over this road. I do not know how far the people of this country will be disposed in the course of time to go, but they must take over this road and run it themselves. That is the simple question; that is the general question. I do not think that the masses of our people are much concerned with the legal refinements which have constituted most of what we have heard in this debate. 1 do not think they are very much concerned about what was the exact legal import of what was in the Bill of three years ago. Why, we departed from that a year ago by giving more money away, and followed on that occasion a course which had support on both sides of the House. I do not mean to say that .it was supported by every one on both sides of the House, but there were a number on both sides who last year departed from the supposed settlement of three years ago, and supported the giving of more money. There is no end to that process.
The great value of the settlement under the process that is proposed by the Government is that the road passes into the hands of the people, and whatever money is put into the road from now on will accrue to

the benefit of the people of Canada themselves.
With regard to the general question of government ownership, I am perfectly certain that a large number of our people are in favour of a trial of the principle. The war has altered men's thinking on this and on a great many other topics. We have found out, under th,e extreme pressure and exigencies of this war, that the state can do things that we did not dream of in our early days of absolute indi-9 p.m. vidualism. We have found out something of what states can accomplish amidst the hardships and trials of war. That has altered men's thinking, and I venture to think that when our soldiers come back, those of them who do come back, by the experience they have had, will prove to our people that they have learned to think, and think deeply, of these national problems. I have met a number of our returned soldiers, and it is surprising to observe the development they have undergone on the intellectual side, and the deep thought they are putting into the problems that confront this nation. They will have an enormous effect upon the thoughts of oiur people and upon the course of our people in regard to these problems.
It is a fact that railroads are owned by many other countries, and are owned and run with success, and if we say that they cannot be owned and run with success by governments in Canada we pass a very severe condemnation upon the public morality of our own people. I want to say further that I fear it is broadly true-and here I know I am voicing the sentiment of a large number of our people and the very best of our citizens-that since Confederation down to the present moment the railroads have owned the country by having a very large ownership in the politicians o.f the country. I value the brave words that fell from the lips of my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. B. B. Bennett) upon that subject the other day, and I want to say that the people of this country know that there was a great deal of truth in his words. It is true that he seemed to concentrate his indignation upon one particular set of railroad operators in the remarks he made upon that subject. I am afraid that those operators are not the only ones who have, to use the word of my hon. friend, debauched young men as that young man on the Pacific coast was debauched. I am afraid all the railroads in Canada are still doing a little

debauching, not only of young men. but also of men who are much older and ought to know a great deal better. It is broadly' true-and we may as well face the fact- that the railroads have owned Canada since Confederation, through owning ou.r politicians. There are a great many people who think the process should be reversed, and that, by Canada owning her railroads and freeing her public men from the evils to which my hon. friend and neighbour from Calgary referred the other day, our public life will be purified, and a development of public spirit in public affairs will take place. I am perfectly confident there is a strong body of opinion behind the principle of government ownership, and that body of opinion, when it is instructed, when it knows what is being done by this legislation, will be behind the Government in these .proposals.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend is entirely in error. The Canadian Northern, like most of the other railroad companies, finances, so far as its rolling stock is concerned, by issuing either directly or indirectly securities against the rolling stock. The modus operandi is this: A railway company desires to buy, let u5 say, $10,000,000 of rolling stock. They pay from twenty to twenty-five per cent in cash, or $2,000,000 to $2,500,000; then they pledge the rolling stock either directly, or, more usually, through a rolling stock company to a trustee.
They issue their securities for $10,000,000 upon these terms. The securities mature at the end of one, two, three, four, five, and so on up to ten or twenty, years. Generally they are not so long as that. In each payment of the debenture there is included a certain amount of principal as well as interest, so that each year an amount of the principal of the rolling stock indebtedness is paid off. When the securities come to an end the rolling stock is all paid for because they have paid not only the interest but the principal. Of course, the rolling stock is, in the meantime depreciating. In the accounts of the Canadian Northern Railway Company there is a statement, showing the amount they have paid on account of principal and interest for rolling stock. That is the system which obtains with scores of large railway companies. It is the favourite and most advantageous way of financing the purchase of rolling stock by railway companies. Rolling stock securities ;are usually considered of a high character because, in the event of a receivership, the receiver has the road to run and he will pay the maturities with respect to rolling stock; otherwise he would lose the rolling stock because the trustee would take it off the system. 1

I appreciate what the Minister of Finance has said in regard to that matter. I know the modus operandi regarding the purchase of rolling stock and the issue of securities of that kind. But I was informed that the rolling stock held by the Canadian Northern was in an altogether different position. It is well that the country should know what the situation is, because I think the people only desire

to know, honestly, frankly and fairly what they are getting and what they are paying for it. So far as I am individually concerned, I am not at all opposed to the people owning the Canadian Northern Railway system-in fact I am rather in favour of it, if it is taken over under a proper method and the people are not paying for it more than it is worth or entering into obligations which will increase the indebtedness of the country to an enormous extent. Our indebtedness is now being increased very rapidly and such an arrangement as is proposed may increase that indebtedness to a greater extent than the credit of the country will stand. It is a question of what we are paying for this property. Then, there is also the question of the system that is to be adopted in operating the property after it is purchased. However, that is a matter that we will have to leave in abeyance until the purchase is made although it too is a question of importance. But, the main question to my mind is: Are we getting a property which is worth the money that we will be obliged to pay for it? The Minister of Finance this afternoon condemned very strongly a proposition to foreclose. He said that the Government is adopting the only system that can be equitably and fairly adopted in taking over this property. I would point out what appears to be a far better way and the way which was suggested, and not only suggested but positively advocated, by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robgrt Borden) in 1914 when this Parliament authorized a guarantee of the bonds of this company to the extent of $45,000,000. As reported in Hansard of 1914, volume 4, page 370, the right hon. gentleman said:
The country, however, may be confronted with conditions in the future which will render prompt and vigorous action necessary. We have made provision for immediate and summary action in case default shall be made-
I apprehend that it is in the mind of every hon. member that default has been made. The Canadian Northern, if not in actual failure to pay, have defaulted by reason of the fact that they have been unable to earn their fixed charges and could not have paid if the Government had not lent them the money to enable them to pay their indebtedness to the Government. The Prime Minister said:
We have made provision for immediate and summary action in case default shall be made.
What does that mean?
The definition of default Is set forth in the 21st clause of the resolution; and, by the 22nd
|Mr. German.]
and subsequent clauses it is, in effect, provided that, if such default takes place-
I assert that such a default has taken place.
-'the Governor in Council may, upon such notice as he deems expedient, declare vacant the offices of the directors' of the Canadian Northern Kailway Company, or of any of the allied companies, and may appoint a new board or boards, upon which very extraordinary powers are proposed to be conferred. Among such powers are the creation of any additional securities, the making of arrangements with the holders of any outstanding securities, and the transfer, with or without compensation, of the Canadian Northern system, or any part thereof (subject to then existing charges) to any corporation created by the Parliament of Canada for the purpose.
There was one method which the Prime Minister stated might be adopted and which, they were providing, should be adopted.
Making of arrangements with the holders of any outstanding securities, and the transfer, with or without compensation, of the Canadian Northern system, or any part thereof (subject to then existing charges) to any corporation created by the Parliament of Canada for the purpose.
Why is that not being done? If that can be done there will be no possible question of the payment to Mackenzie and Mann of the value of the stock. Further:
It is also provided by clause 24 that, if authorized by the Parliament of Canada

That is the section which the Minister of Finance adverted to this afternoon.
-the Governor in Council may, in case of default, declare that the interest of Mackenzie and Mann, in the Canadian Northern Railway system is absolutely barred and foreclosed, and that all the properties and assets thereof, subject to any outstanding obligations, shall thereupon vest in the Crown in the right of the people of Canada,
This is the clause to which the Minister of Finance directed the whole of his argument and it is the clause in regard to which he said that we would be violating the equities if we should take the road over by virtue of it. But I say that we are not bound at all to take over this road under that clause. Then further the Prime Minister goes on:
So if, as apprehended in some quarters, the road cannot, with the assistance now afforded, be brought to a successful conclusion, the Government and Parliament of Canada will have the situation in hand better than by any possible method at the present time.
How are those words being verified in this transaction which the Government is endeavouring, at this late stage of the session, to force through this House-and by their action to-night intend to force

through under closure rules, because there is no reason why the Minister of Finance should have suggested that this clause should stand over and that we should proceed to another clause unless his intention was, as soon as the clauses had all been gone through in this way, to invoke the power of closure and stop discussion.

I shall be ready to retract it all if my suspicions are not well founded.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not think we should get so far as that.

The Prime Minister goes on:
In effect we propose to provide in the first place that a certain amount shall he available for the early and immediate completion of the road, and, if the road is not carried to completion by means of that aid, then the people of Canada, through their Government and Parliament, are enabled in the most effective and vigorous way to grasp the situation, and carry to completion, for their own benefit, one of the great transcontinental railway systems of Canada.
I ask the Finance Minister and the Government and gentlemen who are supporting them to adopt the words of the Prime Minister uttered in 1914, under the clause in that agreement which gives them power so to do, and,
in the most effective and vigorous way grasp the situation and carry to completion for the benefit of the people of Canada one of the great transcontinental railway systems of Canada.
-and do away, obliterate altogether, this idea of paying Mackenzie and Mann five, six, or ten millions of dollars for a stock which the Drayton-Acworth 'Commission have already reported is absolutely valueless. There is no question of foreclosure, there is no question of arbitration. I was chided a few days ago by hon. gentlemen for having at that time supported a resolution providing for arbitration, while I am now suggesting that, whatever is to be paid to Mackenzie and Mann should be fixed by the Chief Justice of the Exchequer Court. As I said that night, and as is borne out by the statement of the Prime Minister, the representation was that that money was sufficient to complete the line and if it did not complete it, then there was an expeditious, effective and complete method of taking over the whole system without paying any more money. The Prime Minister further said:
Some of the features of the agreement should also be called to the attention of the Ho. se.
I am bringing this to the attention of the House and of the country hecause the Finance Minister so particularly emphasized this feature, that there was an equity, a redeemable equity, the value of which should be considered by somebody, he says by arbitration. Now, let us see what the agreement that they entered into at that time provided for. The Prime Minister said:
Some features of the agreement should also be called to the attention of the House. Prominent amongst these is the release of aB claims for contractors' profits, commissions or otherwise, against the Canadian Northern Railway. The provision to which I wish to call attention, and which is, in my opinion, a very important one, will be found on page 19 of the Orders of the Day. That clause reads as follows: ,
"That the contractors"-
Which includes Mackenzie and Mann as a corporation and Mackenzie and Mann individually.
-"will not at any time make or seek to enforce any claim for contractors' profits, commissions, or otherwise against the Canadian Northern, or against any of the constituent or subsidiary companies, upon or in respect of any express or implied contract, understanding, agreement, or stipulation of any kind, heretofore or hereafter made, whereby or whereunder they, or any one or more of them, imay now or hereafter be entitled to receive from the Canadian Northern, or from any of the constituent or subsidiary companies any construction profits, in respect of work heretofore undertaken, or as consideration for transfers of properties, rights of franchises already transferred, or to be transferred under sub-clauses (a) and (b) of this clause, or for commission or remuneration for services in financing, or for any other services heretofore rendered, and all such claims are hereby by them and each of them absolutely renounced and released."
In the face of that statement made by the Prime Minister himself, how in the name of all that is sensible can members of this House, having the interests of the country at heart, representing their constituents as they do, deliberately stand up and vote that, notwithstanding that stipulation by Mackenzie and Mann themselves that they would not at any time thereafter in the event of default make any claim or demand for commissions or for transfers of stock or otherwise under .subclauses (a) and (b)-how, I say, can these gentlemen conscientiously stand up and support the proposition submitted to this House? I bring this to the attention of the House because the agreement itself conclusively answers the statements made by the Finance Minister this evening. He says: you should not expropriate, you should not foreclose,

without taking into consideration the equities which Mackenzie and Mann -have in the property, without taking the valuation of the property, without going into the whole matter, and substance of the physical value, the earning power and otherwise, to arrive definitely at a correct value of this property, and then ascertain whether Mackenzie and Mann -are entitled to compensation. I do not wish to deal harshly with Mackenzie and Mann or any other person, nor do I wish this House to do so; I have a great deal of sympathy for them; they have done a great work, and carried on this enterprise for all these years. But they are no different from other men. To use the venacular of the street, they bit off more than they could chew; they had a bigger enterprise than they could carry through, particularly with this monetary stringency, and the road has become a failure. Other men have failed, and the Government has not come to their rescue. Mackenzie and Mann have been interested in railway building for twenty years or more. This enterprise was started twenty years ago. Every one knows what their situation was then, what it has been since, and what it is to-day; that is a matter of public notoriety. No one need make any suggestion as to what their position is financially and otherwise; it is well known throughout the country. I submit, these men are not fentitled to any .sympathy from this House or from the people of the country. They are entitled to be dealt with fairly, honestly, frankly and justly, and only in that way. In view of the statement made by the Prime Minister three years ago, that there was a speedy, efficacious and complete remedy by taking over this property, and that thero was a release by Mackenzie and Mann of all equities in the property, without a shadow of a claim to be paid anything. I say that we are simply doing justice to the people of this country in standing by the agree-? ment which was made at that time and *saying to these gentlemen:	It is unfortunate for you, we regret we have to do it, but the exigencies of the situation at present make it imperative that we must enforce the obligation imposed in that contract, take that property from you, and put in our own directors; and unfortunately, we will not be able to pay you anything for the difficulties you have encountered and for what you have gone through in those years. I submit that those are views which will .meet with the approval of the people. They are my views at any rate, and I submit them to this House, and I have confidence that 
they will be approved of by the people of. the country generally.
I desire to say a few words-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I was going to move that the committee rise, and that we take up another Bill. If the hon. gentleman from Guysborough wishes to speak now I will give way.

My purpose in asking
leave to say a few words was to reply to the speech of my hon. friend from Red Deer. That hon. gentleman did not deal with the main question before the committee. As I understand it, the question at issue between the two sides of this House is whether we shall pay anything to Mackenzie and Mann for the 600,000 shares of stock we are proposing to acquire. The hon. member for Red Deer did not touch that question. I understand the Government is proposing to pay for that stock at a value to be fixed by arbitration. They do not say how much they are willing to pay, but they are submitting the question to arbitration, which means that they place some value upon the stock. The owners of the stock, I understand, claim that it is worth par, which means that they claim the enormous sum of $60,000,000. It will be for the arbitrators to say whether the people shall pay $60,000,000 for this stock which we, on this side of the House, contend is not worth anything. Our position on this side is quite clear. We say that this stock does not represent any investment; it does not represent a dollar of .money advanced by Mackenzie and Mann or .any one else; it is nothing else than water; that we own it now, under the default made under the conditions of the Act of 1914, and that we are in a position to-day to assume the ownership of that stock without paying any money for it. My hon. friend from Red Deer did not deal with that position at all. He said there was one thing he knew well, and that was that the people of this country are not in favour of shovelling out any more money to Mackenzie and Mann. I was glad to hear him say that, because that is the exact position we take on this side of the House. If these arbitrators decide that the stock is worth $60,000,000, than the people of Canada must shovel out $60,000,000 to Mackenzie and Mann, and the hon. gentleman from Red Deer tells us that the people are not in favour of doing that. I want to place myself on record as opposed to paying anything more to Mackenzie and

Mann for this stock. The hon. member referred to the time when the soldiers would come back. He told us they were doing a lot of thinking, and when they came back they would be interested in the financial affairs of Canada. I believe that is true. They not only have to fight for the existence of (Canada, but they andi their children will have to bear the burden of the public debt. When the soldiers went away there was a public debt of $350,000,000, roughly speaking; -when they come back after this legislation goes through, if it does go through, there will be a debt, independent of the war altogether, of some $800,000,000, and the soldiers will want to know the names of the men who imposed that debt upon them, and upon the people of Canada, and I do not want them to read my name among those who will be on record as having done that.
Will that $800,000,000 be a net debt, or a gross debt?

I regard it as a net debt. The ownership of the road is poor comfort if we have to tax ourselves to pay the interest. If we assume the whole debt of the Canadian Northern, there will be isomewhere in tlie neighbourhood of $800,000,000 independent of the war debt, if we pay all the liabilities connected with the taking over of the company, and I assume we are going to do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are going to own the road.

I object to paying the amount which it is proposed to settle by this arbitration. There is no question in regard to public ownership, as I understand it, between, the two sides of this House. The attitude we take on this side means public ownership just as much as the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite means public ownership, because, if our proposal carries, and the Government takes charge of this stock under the provisions of the Act of 1914, it means that we must assume the existing liabilities of the road, and if we take the stock over by arbitratioh, it means the same thing. The difference is that in one case we shall have to pay whatever the arbitrators decide for the stock, and that will be an addition to the debt of the people of bills country, and that is the part of the debt I particularly object to. It has been said in this House over and over again, that if we take over this property without arbitration it means confiscation.
I want to put myself on record as opposed to that idea. It does not mean confiscation. As I understand it we have a legal right to take this stock now under the Act of 1914. We are not asking for the road. We are not asking for this property. If we had decided to take the property of Mackenzie, Mann and Company and pay them for it, and if we refused to arbitrate and give them its value, that.would be confiscation. That, howeveT, is not what is happening. They are pushing the property on ue. They say: "We cannot keep it ourselves. We cannot carry on. We cannot pay our interest and carry on the business of the road. You must take it off our hands, and you must pay us for it." I think that is an unreasonable proposition, and I think the Government cannot justify itself in taking that stand in face of the legislation of 1914.
