I therefore hope my hon. friend from Rou-ville (Mr. Lemieux) will he able to restrain himself for the present and at some future date give us the benefit of the views he was about to inflict upon tihe committee I move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask to sit again.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: topic
subtopic
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The House again in committee on Bill No. 127, the Military Voters' Act, 1917.- Hon. Mr. Doherty-Mr. Rainville in the Chair.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Is it the intention of the minister to consider the proposed amendments now, or is it his idea simply to submit them, allow us time to go over them, and bring them up to-morrow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
It might be
worth while to run over the amendments, and the sections of the Bill.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The Prime Minister will understand, it was hoped we would get those amendments earlier in the day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Yes, I quite appreciate that.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: It is difficult to insert a word here, and take out a word there offhand, while <we are considering a section. I have a copy of the amendments to be proposed, and I think that as drafted they very correctly represent the discussion we had earlier in the day. But this draft does not seem to contain the amendments which were proposed yesterday. I presume the minister takes it for granted that those amendments are part of the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I am under the impression this contains the amendments that were not adopted yesterday.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I see, for instance, there is very little in this in regard to scrutineers. I think, perhaps, the minister's intention is that the amendments which were proposed yesterday are considered as having been passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: And these are additional amendments?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Yes. If the sections stood they stood as amended.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I think it would be best for the minister to put them on as a notice of motion now, so that hon. members may see what they are.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
In that event I would suggest that we go on with the sections from where we left off, and when we have passed over all the sections of the Bill we may then take up these amendments and others that may possibly arise.

On section 12-Custody and count of ballots:

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I understand that certain amendments are to be proposed by the Minister of Justice. I would suggest that we begin at the first section which is amended, and take the Bill section by section until it is disposed of. It does not seem right to go through a Bill, consider a section, and then pass on to another without finishing the first. One section should be disposed of before proceeding to another. In that way we shall know how to deal with the others, because they are all related.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I certainly understood that the committee reached the understanding last evening that we should go over all the sections first, with a view to receiving suggestions with regard to them, letting them stand as we went along, with a view to passing amendments to meet the suggestions. I had supposed that that understanding would be followed out this evening. Then we should be in a position to go back over the sections that are standing, and, there having in the meantime been opportunity to consider the suggested amendments, we should take up those amendments in their order.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: It is not intended to take up the suggested amendments this evening?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Not unless we reach
them, and unless when we reach them it is possible to deal with them.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I would not like to interfere with any understanding the committee has had, but it strikes me as being very unusual to take up the later sections of the Bill without dealing with and disposing of the former ones, because the determination as to the previous sections of a Bill would influence one in regard to the attitude to be taken as to those later on.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Under the previous section, it is provided that there is to be no polling after eight o'clock of the day fixed for polling in Canada. Is not thirty-one days a very long time in which to get those boxes to London? It seems to me that is deferring the decision of the election for a long time. Under this arrangement it would be probably six weeks from the time the election is held in Canada until there is any finality about it. I realize there will be some difficulty in getting in those

boxes, but I cannot see why that should take thirty-one days.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
There is room, perhaps, for question as to whether the delay may not be too long. It is provided in this section that boxes that have not been received by the thirty-first day, shall not be counted. Inasmuch as we have to cut them off absolutely at the expiry of the delay, it was thought desirable to make quite certain that the delay should be long enough. As to that precise period, I am disposed to place myself in the hands of the committee. If there is error in the delay, it is on the side of its being too long.
With regard to the different subsections of this section, we speak, in various places, of the Secretary of the High Commissioner and likewise of the Canadian Commissioner to France. There is an error in the designation. The proper designation of the officer described as the Secretary of the High Commissioner is the "Secretary of the High Commissioner's Office." That is his proper title. The gentleman described as the Canadian Commissioner to France should be correctly described as the "Com-misssaire General du Canada en France." It appears, by the Order in Council originally constituting the office, that the name was created only in the French language, so that there is no English name properly to designate him. I have separate amendments for each place. Perhaps I might move, in a general way:
That where the word "Commissioner" appears in the section as applied to the Secretary of the High Commissioner at London, there be substituted for it the words "Commissioner's Office", and that wherever the name "Canadian Commissioner to France" appears, there be substituted for it "Commissaire General du Canada en France".

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
What appears to be an omission in subsection 3 of this section is provided for by paragraph (e) of subsection 1 of section 4, which says:
Six scrutineers, three to be appointed on the nomination of the Prime Minister, and three on that of the leader of the Opposition. The appointment shall state the respective addresses at which notices given under this part may be served. One of each nomination may be present on each occasion of the opening of ballot boxes, and at the examination, application and counting of ballots, and every scrutineer shall have and may exercise all the rights of a candidate or his representative at any poll.
I think that is- sufficient, because subsection 3 of section 12 provides that the ballot shall be opened only in the presence of the returning officers and clerks.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I might point out that subsection 1 requires that notice shall be given to the -scrutineers before these operations are begun. As I understood it, notice to scrutineers implied their presence, but it might be better to make it clear by inserting it wherever there is occasion for it.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Why is there so much
delay in counting the ballots? They are not to be counted until the thirty-first day after that fixed for polling in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
The delay is provided
in order to make sure there will be time for all the ballot boxes overseas to reach their destination.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Why not begin to count them as -soon as they come in?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: As the ballots come in the envelopes will be assorted and distributed -among the different constituencies to which they apply. The ballot boxes will be counted when all the boxes are in or on the thirty-first day, which is the time when the axe falls.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
How will the officers '
know when the last ballot box is in? They might not be in within thirty-one days.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
They should all be in
before that. The ' reason why the ballots are not counted immediately they come in is that you would not have all the ballots belonging to a constituency until all the ballots from everywhere had come in and had been assorted. It may be that thirty-one days' delay is too long, but I would rather err on the side of giving perhaps -a little too much time, than risk a number of ballots being left out by making the time too short.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Apart from the time limit fixed for counting, is any other method provided by which it will be known when the ballot boxes are all in?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: By law we assume to be all in on the thirty-first day after the polling day.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Might it- not be wise to provide that the counting may proceed before the thirty-first day if it is found that all the boxes are in? Some record will be kept of the boxes, and it will be known when they are all in.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
That might be done. It might be wise to provide for that if there was reason to think this delay was too long.
If we do that, we shall have to provide that any counting done earlier
10 p.m. than the thirty-first day shall be be done after notice to the scru-

tineers. It has been assumed here that as we were fixing a specific date on which the counting would be done there was no need to provide for notice to the scrutineers, who would have already been notified of the preliminary operations and would be assumed to know when the counting was to take place. If we are to make provision for an uncertain date, it will involve very considerable remodelling and the necessity of a new notice being given.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I think most of the boxes would be in before the thirty-first day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: That is not impossible.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I think there is a great deal of force in what the minister says as to fixing a precise date on which the counting shall take place. The only thing I do not understand is why it should be necessary to allow thirty-one days from the polling day. It would only be a matter of a few hours, I should think, before the ballots in the British Isles would arrive in London, and the ballots on the continent in Paris. It seems to me unreasonable there should be such a long delay.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The thirty-one days does not apply to Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: No, it relates to the proceedings in France and England. I would suggest that this section might perhaps be carried, and we could give a little thought whether it might not be desirable to modify the length of the delay.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: We could let the section carry, on the understanding that we could go back to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
It would be well that we should specifically state the right of the scrutineers to be present, and therefore I would move:
That the subsection be amended, by inserting in the 27th line thereof, after the word "shall" and before the word "open", the words "in the presence of such scrutineers as may attend".

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: It might be well, at the end of subsection 4, to require these statements to be made in triplicate.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: One of these should be delivered to each scrutineer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I have no objection.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
That is the practice in Canada. The deputy returning officer gives a signed statement to.the scrutineer representing each side before he closes the poll. 
It would seem: to be only reasonable to carry out the same provision there.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: If we propose to do that we will have to make it in quadruplicate, beoause the present provision requires him to hand a duplicate to the secretary of the High Commissioner and to the Commissioner to France. If we want to provide copies for the scrutineer of each side we would have to have four altogether. I suppose he may give copies.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Yes, he may give copies- "and shall deliver copies thereof to each scrutineer present."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I beg to move:
That subsection 4 be amended by inserting at the end thereof: "Copies of such statements shall be delivered to the scrutineers in attendance."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to, and subsection 4 as amended agreed to.
On section 12, subsection 5-Vote for a party counted as vote for a recognized candidate:

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The word "party" there, of course, refers to "political party" in lines 6, 7, 8, and elsewhere?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Yes, I think it is fairly clear from the context in the other provision. In view of the provision of the ballot for "Government," "Opposition" and "Independent candidate," we might insert the words "Labour party." If we insert those words, there is no purpose in stating "other party," because it will not be possible to mark a ballot for any party except the party that figures on the ballot paper. Therefore, I beg to move:
That subsection 5 be amended by striking out, in the 49th line, the word "other" and substituting the word "Labour."

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: It is to be observed that if there is to be a delay until this official recognition is given by the leaders of both parties it will delay the casting of the votes on the other side? The subsection provides that this recognition shall take place within five days after the nomination, You will have to communicate with Great Britain. How are you going to communicate to the soldier the names of the official candidates?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
We have made special
provision for the notification of that recognition. We have taken means to have immediately communicated to the soldiers the names of the candidates proposed. If the

soldier does not know the name of the man whom, say, the leader of the Opposition has designated as the candidate of his party, he is quite sure of getting his vote applied to the candidate by simply voting for the Opposition. This is only for the purpose of identifying the man to whom will go the votes that are given to the Opposition. We must give some delay for these gentlemen after nomination to determine their respective candidates, and I do not think that any serious evil results if we do not make special provision for communicating that to the soldiers.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Suppose that it should happen that the Prime Minister was unable to state the candidate recognized by him? It would hardly be possible, but it might happen that there would be two candidates nominated, both of whom were supporting him. They might both be Independent Conservative candidates. What would be done with votes cast for the Independent? Of course a voter can protect himself by voting for the individual, but I suppose that many votes would be lost if what I state happened.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
If a man votes for the
Government and the Government has no candidate, there is no means by which we can transfer that vote to any candidate.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Is there not opportunity for infinite confusion and conflict in this section? It says within five days of the day of nomination the Prime Minister and the leader of the Opposition and the recognized leader of any Independent party." There may be several parties, and there may not be a recognized leader for each. There may be the parties that o.ur press friends speak of that are being incubated every day at the Chateau Laurier. There may be any number of parties with no ability to recognize -a leader. If that continues up to the election, how will the votes be counted?
Mr. DOHERTY':	I do not see how you
could meet such a case.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: How would it work out in a constituency where a person of independent views runs 'who is acceptable to the Government because his views on what is recognized as the outstanding issue, namely, conscription, are acceptable to the Government? If there were two candidates, one conscriptionist Liberal and one straight, common Liberal, how would they be distinguished? Would the conscriptionist Liberal be called a Government candidate?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: It would depend upon what the Prime Minister or the leader of the Opposition would say.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Suppose both claimed
him?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: All the happier for the candidate who gets bath the Government and the Opposition vote.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The Prime Minister and -the leader of -the Opposition might trade off one for the other.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Let us suppose that
there are two men running neither of whom is ideal to the respective leaders, the Prime Minister saying: I am not going to have that man on my list because, for certain reasons, I do not want him, even if he does support conscription,-
Mr. PUGSLEY': He might be a free trader.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: -would there be no allocation of votes for that man at all?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The votes will be thrown away in that case.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Then the candidates are really driven to receive the endorsation of one party or the other.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: In this sense, that Opposition votes cannot be counted for any candidate unless he has bean recognized by the leader of -the Opposition and, similarly, votes cast for the Government cannot be counted for any candidate unless he has been recognized by the leader of the Government. -

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I move to amend the [DOT]section by inserting in the third line of page 10, after the word "independent" the words " or Labour party."

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Do I understand the effect of .this section to be that the names of candidates are to be cabled to Great Britain and the list of them will be sent to 'he different camps and the recognition is to be commuinicated' within five days after the official nomination? What is to be done with that so far as sending it to the other side is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: We have no express provision for its being sent to the other side at that time. It does not come to tie required until we are allotting the ballots and we assume that would be known to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. -

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
What is the objection to placing on the ballot "member of the Conservative party" and "member of the Liberal party" instead of using the words "Government" and "Opposition." We hear so much about other governments that we can never tell whether anybody can support any government; it may not be in vogue about the time the vote is taken. I think that, in the interest of party government, the parties should he named there without any disrespect to anybody in the House, we all see every morning that we are to have a new government. One gentleman has been given the making of governments in this country and he has been busy for about two months. This House has been sitting by waiting for this Government to come through and I do not think there is a single soldier in the trenches who would feel inclined to vote for any government that this gentleman would bring forth. I refer to Sir Clifford Sifton. Sir Clifford Sifton, as we all know, has figured in the courts during the last year.
It was shown he was the recipient of about a million francs, which, as a middleman, he squeezed out of the French Government and French people for whom we are sending our soldiers to fight. In the interest of the people of this country let us have the names of the parties there, so that the soldiers will know what party they are voting for. I am a Conservative, and don't make any bones about it, and I think the Conservative party is the party in this war, that party will win the fight that is coming on. and we had better put that name at the top of the column.
Mr. A. K. (MACLEAN: Put it in the statute.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I am a Tory, and the other parties are Liberals, with all due respect to them.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I.f I understand the suggestion^ it is that the words "Government" and " Opposition " should 'be struck out, and a space left for the name of the candidate. I was going to suggest the same thing. I do not think there is any advantage in this great departure of allowing the ballot to be cast for Government, Opposir tion or Independent candidate. We had better pursue the old practice of having the names of the candidate placed on the ballot. Let the elector write the name of the .person for whom he wants to vote. I see no reason to make the change.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
In this election there
will not be the clean-cut cleavage between

the parties which formerly existed. Our friends in. the trenches simply have the knowledge which they possessed when leaving here, and I think it is a fair presumption that they have not at their fingers ends details of things that have happened during the last few months, and we know that throughout the whole of Canada men who were keen opponents of one party at one time are no longer in that class, and might be altogether out of sympathy, in a want of confidence motion, with their party. What my hon. friend has said with regard to the government to. be formed by Sir (Clifford Sifton, if there was any injustice done to any person because of that, *if the boys at the front would resent it, I suppose another notice could be published of those not under his wing, and I think this list would be the one that would be favoured more toy the soldiers. In justice to Sir 'Clifford Sifton, the sum of money which he made out of the French Government was made in a horse trade, and it was well laid down policy of this Government that the finer rules and principles of life do not prevail with reg.ard'to horse trading. This was shown in the Kings county horse deals.
With regard to the .money Sir Clifford Sifton made, we .must remember that fact, and judge him as we would judge any other man desiring to make money as a horse trader. I very strongly endorse the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John that the names of the candidates be inserted. I was going to further suggest, because there will be a great absence of information in the minds of the electors, that a certain number of geographical maps be printed by the department, and that these be available to the soldiers also. Each province might be divided into electoral districts on the maps.
I do not know so much about any part of the country except my own, and I know that the redistribution has transformed the district, for example, so that hundreds of men who used to live in the Moosejaw electoral district have no idea what riding they are in. It is divided into four complete ridings, and parts of other ridings taken in. These men would have no accurate knowledge as to the ridings in which they should vote. Can the Minister of Justice inform us if there are any electoral geographical maps?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
They are furnished by the clerk o.f the Crown in Chancery to all the officers who are doing the counting and assorting, and it is precisely on account of that fact that it is important for men to vote for Government, Opposition, or Inde-

pendent candidate, because an elector, such as the one described by the hon. gentleman, one who is not quite certain of the electoral district to which he belongs, might vote for a man of a particular name, but if he has made a mistake in the electoral district to which the vote belongs, and puts in the name of the candidate of whatever party he desires to vote for, his 'ballot will be lost. Whereas with this ballot, you have an advantage, because the man who is uncertain as to his constituency marks his ballot Government or Opposition, as he sees proper,'and care is taken to see that the vote goes to the candidate in the constituency in which that man is entitled to vote. It is a great protection for the voter against the consequence of error, as to constituencies, and, with the best precaution that can be taken, errors will, I fear be very prevalent.
Subsection 6-Vote for person by name accepted if he is a candidate:

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: It seems to me that, under this section, there might be some considerable injustice. I think it should be provided that, in the event of a person being a candidate in an electoral district other than that to which, in accordance with the endorsement or marking on the envelope, such ballot had been applied, and if there appeared a bona fide intention of voting for that candidate, such candidate should not be deprived of the vote. Provision should be made to rectify a clear mistake.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I do not see how we could rectify it. If a man has a vote in one electoral district, and he votes for a man who is a candidate in some other district, he is not a qualified voter in that district. I think it is impossible to meet the case suggested by the hon. gentleman.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I think that if the hon. member for Welland will consider the matter he will see that his suggestion might lead to a great injustice. You might take a constituency that was strong one way or the other, where a man's vote was not needed very badly, he could simply transfer his vote to the next constituency. I am afraid it would open the door to things many of us would not like to see. He must state to the officer under oath where his residence is, and if he is not sure about it, under section 12, subsection 2, they will look over electoral charts and make up their minds where that man resides, and where he should vote.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: You might as well abolish all those provisions, if that suggestion were adopted.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: A man ought to be compelled to vote only for a candidate representing his electoral district.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The other evening a question was raised in regard to the mutilation of a ballot. If it should happen that a man wrote on the ballot the name of the candidate for whom he voted-he being a voter in the electoral district for which that man was a candidate but at the same time marks a cross after either " Opposition " or " Government," what would happen to the ballot? I think there was general agreement that if he wrote in the name of the Opposition candidate and also put a cross after " Opposition " he would only have doubly clearly expressed what he wanted, and the (ballot should be counted for the Opposition candidate.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: But suppose he did it the other way?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
There is where the question arose. Supposing a man voted expressly by name for a candidate who was a candidate in the constituency in which he was a voter-say he voted by name for a gentleman who was a Government candidate, and put a cross after " Opposition." I think in the absence of any provision on the subject that ballot would have to be rejected, because the man would have voted for tooth sides. It was urged with a great deal of force that the expression by which a man had voted for a candidate by name should be taken as clearly indicating his real intention, and that the ballot should not be set aside merely because by some possible mistake he port this cross after the name of the other party. I was very much impressed with that. I think all the presumptions are that that man clearly intended to vote for the individual whose name he put down, but was in error as to what party that individual represented. To meet that view I move to amend subsection 6 by adding the following words:
"Where any ballot paper bears on Us face a vote for a person by name and is also marked as a vote for a party other than that of which such named person is a candidate, such ballot shall be counted as a vote 'for the candidate named thereon."

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I do not think that should be, because there you have the name of the candidate, and you have the

man putting a cross in the square opposite the party which that candidate does not represent. As an illustration, he is voting for a man who is a Government candidate, and then he puts the cross in the Opposition square. What right would these returning officers have to say that he intended to vote for the Government candidate any more than he intended to vote for the Opposition, or vice versa? It seems to me in a case of that kind the ballot would have to be rejected. In case a man were to put the name of the candidate and then put a cross in the square of the party the candidate represented-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
In that case I would
make no provision, because none is needed.
Mr. PUG'SLEY: Surely it would not do in the other instance, because it would be entirely uncertain as to how the man intended to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: It was urged with a good deal of force that we must endeavour to ascertain the intention of the voter, and carry it out. While unless you make a provision in the law about it, the reasoning of the hon. member for St. John would lead to the conclusion that you must reject the ballot. I think, with all respect, that all the presumptions in that case are that where the mistake occurred was not with regard to the individual this man named but with regard to the name of the party to which that individual belonged. It ie well to remember that though we talk about parties, and Opposition, and Government, after all in an election in each constituency what is sought to be determined is, what man has the majority of the votes? Here you have the express declaration of the intention to vote for the man, and I would feel -^although I am not disposed to insist upon it-that we were quite justified in saying that rather than reject the ballot we would count it for the man for whom, there is such a very strong presumption, the voter intended to vote. I may say there were quite a number of members here the other evening, who are not now present, who entertained that view.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to, and subsection as amended agreed to.
On subsection 7-Ballot not rejected for uncertainty if intention of voter can be seen on mere inspection :

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I would like to ask the minister if I am correct in assuming that no mark is to be placed on the ballot [Mr. Pugsley.}	I
by the officer taking the vote in Europe? Should not there be a direction that when the ballot is handed out it should be marked by the officer in charge, so that it can be identified when it comes back?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
What we relied upon for
getting back the identical ballot that was given out was the fact that the marking was to be done in the presence of the officer. If you insist upon markings, signatures, .and so forth, you will indispose the soldier to engage in this thing. We have to simplify it as much as we can.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 13-Duty of every returning officer under part III to send certificate, ballots, etc., to general returning officer:

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: If a recount were demanded of a poll within Canada, how would those ballot boxes, ballots and other papers be procured? In the meantime, they would have been sent to Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The provision is that the returning officer does not send forward those papers until the delay for asking for a recount has expired.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The delay 13 for how many days?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Four days.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The numbers might be given, but it might take two weeks to get the documents.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Once notice of demand for a recount is given, the returning officer should not send them away pending a proceeding. He does not send them away until he has made the 'final addition of the votes.
On section 14-Declaration of election by general returning officer:

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I think we should
provide for verification of'the cable. Otherwise, we might have the returning officer returning a member for a certain constituency who might afterwards be unseated owing to an error in the cable.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I suppose a
mistake of that kind could be corrected without any special provision. Of course, a telegram is liable to error, and so is a letter. I remember being told a very interesting incident by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery when I was a very much younger member of this House than I am now. He said that happening to look up some documents, purely ;by accident, I think, relating to a particular election,

after the parliamentary term had expired for which the election took place, he discovered that through a mistake in a return by one of the returning officers the man who had been returned was not actually elected, but was returned and sat for the whole parliamentary term. So accidents are possible under any system. What my hon. friend suggests is that we should have some better means of verification than by a telegram. The only difficulty about that is the delay it would occasion. The delay has already been alluded to by the hon. member for Carleton (Mi4. Carvell).

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Is it not correct that the cablegram is only for public information? Must not the returning officer await the statements before making the declaration, as provided in subsection 4 of section 12?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Yes. I was
rather misled by 'the suggestion of iny hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). The telegram is only for publio information, and the formal return must be made later.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: >1 was going to suggest that we follow the same practice in regard to the verification of the announcement of the results as was provided by an amendment yesterday with regard to the verification of the names of the candidates sent to Great Britain. The names must be cabled back for verification. I am only suggesting that the cable should be verified before the announcement is made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
As the cable is
only for public information, perhaps we might leave it to the discretion of the, officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: All these things, if 1 am not mistaken, are officially announced in the' Gazette. What I had in mind was that this sort of information will be so generally known that any error in a telegram would correct itself, because people will have the information from other sources. But I have no objection to having the telegram repeated.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Suppose the steamer went down with the returns-some ballots nearly went down on the Lusitania-the telegram might be the sole basis on which to make the returns. Is any provision made in case the returns are destroyed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: No special provision is made, but the general rule would apply, that where the best evidence is destroyed you couM resort to secondary evidence.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The certificates are to be given to each party.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Yes. They are in duplicate. The High Commissioner keeps one,, and sends one over here.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: This is a new law and abrogates the old in regard to the return of members of Parliament. Suppose that the authentic and official documents on which the returning officer makes his return are lost. My hon. friend says, take the next best evidence, as at common law.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The same thing would apply.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: You cannot act without a statutory provision.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
The High Commissioner gets the return in duplicate and sends one over here. If that one gets lost
11 p.m. he has the other one. It is a duplicate, not a mere copy. It is as much the original statement as the one that was lost.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I quite understand that, but what is the returning officer in Canada going to do in,the meantime without any returns?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The provision is that he does not announce the election till he gets the returns. We are providing against the first statement being lost on its way over, by having a duplicate in the High Commissioner's office. I suppose we could provide, if it is really thought necessary, that under those circumstances, the returns can be established by secondary evidence; that is, by producing copies or evidence of another sort.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I submit in all seriousness that if this question of the return of members of Parliament was reviewed in the courts it would turn entirely on the construction of the statutes, and if there was no provision for the returning officer making the return upon secondary evidence the return would be set aside on the ground that he had no authority to make it. There is another thing that should be remembered. Suppose there is any postponement i or delay in the forwarding of returns. That might mean that the return of all the members to the House of Commons would be delayed, because we are all in the same boat. The returning officer cannot act until he gets the returns, and the returns may be delayed for an indefinite period owing to an accident.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I do not think anything could be done to meet that, un-

less we were to provide for an indefinite number of originals to be filed with the High Commissioner. The minister has gone so far as to provide duplicates. If one is lost the other is there. You will be in a position either to use that duplicate or to give secondary evidence of it.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: You would need to say so in the statute. It may be that the return for every hon. member of this House might be delayed indefinitely unless you state in the statute that in the event of the loss of the return the contents of the duplicate may be verified in some way, and the return made.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: We might perhaps treat that section as we have treated some others. I will think the matter over.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 15, subsection 1-Final addition and recount in London of votes polled in United Kingdom or Europe:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: This section gives an answer to the question which was asked in connection with section 13.	[DOT]

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Are we to understand that the only way in which any one can get a remedy by means of a recount is to have the recount in England and to incur the expense that such a proceeding will involve? Why cannot these ballots be sent to Canada and be recounted here, if necessary? A candidate who desires a recount will have to retain English counsel, and a man who desires to avail himself of that remedy will need to have a bank behind him.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The difficulty is the danger of the ballots being lost under present conditions.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I think it would be worth while taking some chance about that. Anybody who knows anything about retaining solicitors and counsel in England knows what an expensive matter it is. This applies to hon. gentlemen on both sides. Surely some remedy could be had in Canada. Any one connected with the legal profession knows what it means. Any hon. gentleman, who is not a lawyer and who wants to have any question brought up, must retain Canadian counsel, the Canadian counsel must communicate with some solicitor in England and then this solicitor must hire counsel to attend these hearings. It is a tremendously onerous proposition. Surely there ought to be some provision for a recount in Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Of course, the election is being conducted under extraordinary conditions, and we cannot have in England or France the same conditions as those which prevail in Canada. It is purely a question of whether you shall have the delay and danger of transmitting these ballots to Canada or whether you shall have a recount in Great Britain. It is a question for the committee.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
It is not a party
question. It is a question in which every member of this House is interested. If there is any mistake, or if there is any question that a candidate for this Bouse wishes to have investigated, he might as well understand that he cannot have a recount in Canada but that he must go to tremendous expense, so much so that he cannot have a recount unless he has a large amount of money.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I think my hon. friend's idea of the additional expense is somewhat exaggerated. You would not require counsel. A solicitor in England would do all the work. Solicitors in Great Britain do a good deal of work in the courts under the modern practice'there. There is no need to retain counsel unless someone wants to go to that additional expense. All you would require would be some junior solicitor to attend for the purpose of seeing that these ballots, if they had been properly marked, had been counted.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Look at the procedure :
shall be instituted and had at London, England, before a person who may be designated for the purpose by a judge of the High Court of Justice of England. Such proceedings shall be initiated by an application to the High Commissioner or Acting High Commissioner of Canada at London that he secure the appointment of a recounting authority.
There is no compulsion on him to secure it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: We have to depend, in this respect, upon the comity of nations to a certain extent, upon the expectation that the judges in Great Britain will act in conformity to what after all is only a request. I have no doubt that tihe judges in England would assist in carrying out the Act. We really have not jurisdiction to tell them to do so. We have every confidence that they will act in the manner suggested and assist us to carry out the Act.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
If an hon. member of this House finds he is twenty or thirty votes behind he will want a recount. How is he

to get it? It says here that such application shall be made -within four days after the time fixed in the Canada Gazette and the London Times. Is he to move by affidavit?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I want to see the procedure.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: After the judge has appointed a person to discharge the duties which the county court judges discharge in this country, the procedure will be the same; either he or some one on his behalf will have to make an affidavit, I suppose.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: There are some very dose decisions in regard to what is sufficient for affidavits for recounts.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
By section 15 all the provisions of part 3 with regard to recounting are made applicable, with the substitution for the word " judge," of the words " recounting authority." You make application to the High Commissioner, you ask him to get a recounting authority appointed, and when he is appointed you proceed before him just as before a judge here. Power is conferred upon the recounting authority to extend for such reasonable periods as may be necessary the times limited for taking any step in official addition or recounting proceedings affecting any votes polled under this Bill.
Mr. A. >K. MACLEAN: Part 3 of our Act gives four days between the opening of the returning officer's court and the commencement of recounting proceedings. *

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: There is authority to extend the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
The Governor in Council is empowered to fix a date from which the four days will count. .
I wish to move the same amendment that has been made to section 12. I shall move in respect to this group of clauses, that, wherever the words " secretary of the High Commissioner of Canada " appear, there shall be substituted the words " secretary of the High Commissioner's office," and that wherever the words " Canadian Commissioner to France " appear, there be substituted the words " Commissaire General du Canada en France."

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Is any attempt being made under this law to forward these ballots to Canada? Under the law of to-day
30fk
an affidavit must be made of incorrect statement or improper adding, and it must be made positive. It seems to me that part 3 would have to be amended in regard to the deposit. This provision applies to Quebec and Alberta and the Yukon. Do I understand that no deposit is to be required for a recount on the other side?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: We have provided that all those provisions contained in part 3 shall be applied, and that the recounting authority shall be the equivalent of a judge. I would understand that to mean that when you go before that recounting authority you must satisfy him you are complying with the requirements of the law.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: With whom are you going to deposit the money? There are special officers referred to in part 3, but no provision with regard to this. Part 3, of the statute refers to the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I would think that it would be quite within the power of the recounting authority to say: "If you do not make the necessary deposit, the recount will not go on."

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Deposit with whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
The recount authority. We have to adapt conditions over there, and I do not think there is very much doubt that we, having transmitted this duty to the recount authority, he could act. We cannot send all these officers over from Canada, but the substantial obligation to make the deposit exists, and I do not think it would be any excess of power of the recounting authority to require that the deposit be made. He could find somebody reliable with whom to make the deposit.
Mr. MACDONALD We make part 3 applicable to conditions in England, but how will the deposit be made? In some provinces in Canada we deposit the money with the Clerk of the Court; in other provinces it is deposited with somebody else. You do not say anything as to who shall hold the deposit in England. If you are going to provide for security for costs, you should provide where the money shall be deposited otherwise the judge in England designated for this purpose would very fairly say: "There is no provision with regard to security for costs here." The statute should be made clear. A party might lose his recount, after going to a lot of expense, if the deposit were not made properly. Applications for recount in Can-



ada are set aside when deposits are not properly made.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
In order that there may be no difficulty we might add to subsection 2 the following words:
And the recounting authority shall have power to determine with whom the deposit described shall be made.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: There is apparently no way of a candidate learning the result of the count in England, or in Europe, unless he has an agent at hand, who would communicate that information to him. The result is not telegraphed to Canada until the final counting, which can only be after the recount, if there is one. I cannot suggest a way out of the difficulty, but the candidate in Canada has no means of determining whether or not he should ask for a recount.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
If we go back to the
section that deals with it, the provision is that when the counting is completed the counting officer hands a certificate of the result of that counting to the High Commissioner in England, who telegraphs it at once to the general returning officer, and follows that up by sending over his statement, and the returning officer, upon that statement, is empowered to proclaim the result of the election. There is no provision to send to levery candidate in Canada notice of what that counting is. It would seem to me it might be fairly assumed that, when all that information is communicated to the general returning officer here, and is furthermore in the hands of the scrutineers representing the respective parties upon the other side, there would be no real difficulty in a candidate ascertaining it. I have not the slightest doubt that that information will be public property in Canada the day after the telegram comes.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: What section requires a telegram to be sent to Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Subsection 9 of section 12, which reads:
(9) Upon receipt of the statement, mentioned in subsection four of this section, of the votes applicable to each candidate in an electoral district, the secretary of the High Commissioner and the Canadian Commissioner to France, respectively, shall communicate the text thereof by telegraph, and such document itself by registered post, to the general returning officer.
Immediately on the statement being sent in, it will be cabled to this country, and followed by sending the statement by mail.

Then, as we amend subsection 4 of section 12, it will require that copies of such statements-that is the statement of the result of the counting-shall be delivered to the scrutineers in attendance.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I do not see how it can be improved, but there is not much chance of a candidate asking a recount in four days.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Section 14 makes it the duty of the general returning officer, when he receives the information here, to communicate it to any person who asks for it.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: That means he will make it public.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: And a candidate has only to ask for it, and he will get it.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Does the Minister of Justice understand that these provisions with regard to recount do not affect the right to a recount being had in Canada, with respect to the votes being cast in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I do not think it possible that those conditions could deprive the candidate of the right to have a recount of the ballots cast in Canada.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Would you put in a saving clause? You have one general returning officer. Your returning officer in each county does not return anybody. There should be some amendment to part 3, in order to make it clear you could serve a returning officer in a certain time. How would a man in British Columbia serve the returning officer in Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
The obligation of the
ordinary returning officer at home is to send all his papers to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. We have substituted the obligation to send them to the general returning officer. We have left the rest of the law as it was. The provision stands entirely unaffected, hut that operation will be stopped if somebody makes an application to the judge for a recount. All we have done with part 3 is to make its provisions applicable overseas, with the substitution of these different things, but we have not made them inapplicable to the operations here carried on under part 3, and those operations remain subject to the provisions of part 3.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: If the minister will assure me that if after looking into' this matter I have any suggestions to make it clear I shall have the right to make them-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: If I should be in error about it, I shall be glad to have it brought to my attention.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 16-Emergency poll:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
There is a printer's
error which I would like to correct. I think the word " be " should be inserted at the beginning of the third line, and I move that the section be amended in that respect.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The Governor in Council might be called upon very unexpectedly to grant a poll. I think the section should require notice to the candidates at least. It might happen that you would not have time even to put up notices. I know the British Columbia vote at Halifax was taken on less than twenty-four hours' notice, and a great many did not know it was being held.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The Governor in Council is empowered to make provision for the polling of the vote. I think there are not apt to be very many cases in which this will arise, and I believe the Governor in Council may be entrusted to make reasonable provision.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: There is nothing in this section to the effect that the provisions which will be hereinafter enacted regarding the scrutineers being present shall be adhered to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I should think the Governor in Council would consider that in making provision for the holding of the vote on a different date. I do not understand that it would alter the matter of holding the poll.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Except that he
might not have time to carry it out at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: If there is not time to carry it out at all, I suppose the Governor in Council would not try it. All he is empowered to do is to make provision for the polling of their votes in the manner by this part provided. He cannot change the manner.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Read the balance of the section.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
(Reading):
On a day prior to their departure, and may modify the provisions of this part relating to time or procedure in so far as may be necessary to render such polling possible.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I think the question for the committee is whether under those exceptional conditions it is willing to entrust the Governor in Council to provide to meet them. If it is not, of course I do not know how we can very well deal with it. I am willing to insert any words that may be useful.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I only mention it so that the attention of the minister may be drawn to it.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Will this Act apply to home guards, where there are home regiments?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: It would apply to the militia on active service. Militia on active service may be away from their homes just the same as the Canadian Expeditionary Force.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 17-Offences and penalties:

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Of course, this section is of no. value unless there is some amendment to the Militia Act by which the doing of these things would be a military offence. It could not be enforced outside the country. I suggest to the minister whether we could amend the Militia Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: It strikes me as a somewhat remarkable thing to try to make these duties military duties. While it is quite true that if the offences be committed outside of Canada we will not be able to apply the punishment-at least I take that to be the law-it is also true that those things may be brought about by people who are in Canada, although the operation itself is actually effected outside of Canada. Those parties in Canada would be subject to the punishment. Then we must remember that this statute also has application in Canada for the taking of military votes in Canada. As to the suggestion that we should make this offence a violation of military duty, it would certainly be extreme to apply it to people who are not military officers.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
It would be of no value to those who were not military officers nor attached to the force. This may be only mere ornamentation and intended to apply only to stray persons in Canada, who may be connected, in some way or another, with the force; but suppose men connected with the taking of the votes in England or France found that some fraud had been

committed, there is no way in which any penalty could be imposed on them, unless the minister would amend the Militia Act 'so that anything made an offence under this measure could be dealt with by the military authorities. The trouble about the whole thing is that military offenders can not be punished unless the Imperial authorities pass some complementary legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
The whole proceeding is distinctly a civilian affair, and it seems to be rather unfair to seek by our law to make a man who happens to be a military officer amenable for an offence for which a civilian doing the same thing would not be amenable. If the hon. gentleman will look over the section he will find that many more of those things can be done in Canada than he conceives. People in Canada,
- for instance, may seek to prevent the delivering of those messages. This provision is far from being mere ornamentation.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: It simply means this, that anything in the way of infraction of the law that can be committed may be committed in England and France, and nothing will be done to the party who commits the offence. Will the minister see if he can find some way of carrying out my suggestion?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I shall be glad to think about that as well as about other matters. At first glance it strikes me as an extraordinary proposition that we should make offences of this kind military offences.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: So far as I am able to understand the suggestion of my hon. friend, I do not think it would advance the matter one whit further.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I make the suggestion only as a possible solution. There is no sense in inserting in this Military Voters' Act a quantity of fanciful infractions of the -law, and penalties, and things of that kind if they are to .be only of as much value as waste paper. Can not something better be devised?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend is mistaken. This section has an application in Canada and therefore, it is not purely ornamentation. Outside of Canada, it has at least a certain moral effect; it is there on the statute book. If we should attempt to convert offences of this kind into military offences, we would simply be attempting to evade 'the plain provisions of the Militia Act and the corresponding Act
[Mr Macdonald.]
in the United Kingdom to which, in the final analysis, we have to resort for the enforcement of military law.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
You might make ad
these men honourary colonels and bring them under the Militia Act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: In efiect, what my hon. friend would suggest is this, that we should make offences under this measure offences under the statute of the United Kingdom. If we enact that, we would not be a bit further along, because the same objection that might be raised to this could be raised with regard to that.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I do not think so. I think that under our statute relating to military matters, the King's regulations are made effective in Canada and applicable to the forces. The King's regulations are in force in Canada, because it is so stated in the Militia Act. I simply want to suggest consideration of the question as to whether or not something can be done.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Section agreed to.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Will soldiers have to vote in their capacity of soldiers? There must be some hundreds of soldiers employed in the city of Ottawa, and the same is true of other cities. They will have a vote in their capacity of civilians as well as in their capacity of soldiers. Will those men have an opportunity of voting in either capacity; that is, can they vote as citizens or vote as soldiers?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The soldier may exercise either vote. He cannot, of course, exercise both.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Is there any provision by which a soldier can go home and vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: We are trying under this measure to make provision so that the soldier away from home will have the poll brought to him. We are, therefore, not making a provision to let him go home to vote. He votes for his own constituency, but he votes, under this system, in his camp or wherever he is. If he happens to be at his home, he may vote there.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I would suggest that
the minister give notice of these amendments and then, between now and to-morrow, we could take them into consideration and try to frame a measure as it will be with these amendments. If all the amendments were comprised in this typewritten document, the matter would not be too bad, but certain amendments have

already been adopted. I suppose, if we take Hansard of yesterday and these proposed amendments, we shall find out how the legislation reads.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Before we deal with that matter, the ballot form and also forms B and D require amendment.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The hon. member for St. John notified me before leaving that his constituency is not described correctly. It should be "the City and Counties of St. John and Albert.''

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
The electoral districts affected are St. John, Ottawa, Halifax, South Cape Breton and Richmond. I beg to move that:
Form A be amended by striking out in line three after the word "particular," the word "person" and substituting the words "candii date or candidates designated by name,"' and by striking out the word "person" after the word "such" in the fourth line thereof and substituting the words "candidate or candidates." Further, by striking out the words "une per-sonne en particulier" in the seventh line thereof, after the word "pour" and substituting therefor the words "un ou des candidats en particulier designCs par ieurs noms" and by striking out in the eighth line the words "cette personne" after the word "de," and substituting therefor the words "ce ou cea candidats." By inserting in clear black type, the words "in the electoral dictricts of Ottawa, Halifax, South Cape Breton and Richmond, and the city and counties of St. John and Albert, two candidates may be voted for"- Dans les divisions Electorates d'Ottawa, Halifax, Cap-Breton Sud et Richmond, et St. Johnj on peut voter pour deux candidats." By erasing the straight line in' the first space. By1 making a fifth white space and inserting the words "I vote for the Labour candidate"-. "Je vote pour le candidat Ouvrier."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I beg t-o move that Form D be amended by adding to the last word thereof the words, "I have not previously voted at this election."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I would suggest to the minister that No. 1 space should be wider. It will be remembered that in four instances two names may have to be written within that space.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Perhaps we might have that done.
Progress reported.
On motion of Sir Robert Borden, the House adjourned at 12.05 a.m. Friday.
Friday, August 24, 1917.
